options.text: Use Firebase Realtime Database for ingestion and storage, and Cloud Run functions for processing and analytics.
Use Cloud Data Fusion for ingestion and transformation, and Cloud SQL for storage and analytics.
Use Pub/Sub for ingestion, Dataflow with Apache Beam for processing, and BigQuery for storage and analytics.
Use Cloud Storage for ingestion, Dataproc with Apache Spark for batch processing, and BigQuery for storage and analytics.

questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub provides scalable, reliable ingestion for continuous event streams. Dataflow with Apache Beam performs low-latency stateful stream processing, including session windows and aggregations, and uses event-time watermarks, triggers, and allowed-lateness settings to handle out-of-order and late data. BigQuery is a suitable analytical store for the processed clickstream data.

**Learn more:** [Architectural overview of Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/architecture) · [Streaming pipelines](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-pipelines)

A web server publishes click events as messages to a Pub/Sub topic. The server includes an `eventTimestamp` attribute in each message that records when the click occurred. You have a Dataflow streaming job that reads this Pub/Sub topic through a subscription, performs some transformations, and writes the results to another Pub/Sub topic for the advertising department.  
  
The advertising department must receive every message within 30 seconds of its corresponding click, but reports that messages arrive late. Your Dataflow job has system lag of about 5 seconds and data freshness of about 40 seconds. Inspection of several messages shows no more than 1 second of lag between `eventTimestamp` and `publishTime`. What is the issue, and what should you do?

options.text: The advertising department is causing delays when consuming the messages. Work with the advertising department to fix this.
Messages in your Dataflow job are taking more than 30 seconds to process. Optimize your job or increase the number of workers to fix this.
The web server is not pushing messages fast enough to Pub/Sub. Work with the web server team to fix this.

questions.explanation:
Data freshness measures the difference between an element’s event time and processing time; a value of about 40 seconds shows that some elements are being processed too late to meet a 30-second requirement. The approximately 1-second delay before Pub/Sub publication does not account for the lateness, so the pipeline requires performance optimization or additional worker capacity.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow job metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/using-monitoring-intf) · [Troubleshoot slow or stuck streaming jobs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/troubleshoot-slow-streaming-jobs)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run a logistics company and want to make event delivery from vehicle-based sensors more reliable. You operate small data centers worldwide to capture these events, but the leased lines connecting your event-collection infrastructure to your event-processing infrastructure are unreliable and have unpredictable latency. You want to resolve this in the most cost-effective manner. What should you do?

options.text: Deploy small Kafka clusters in your data centers to buffer events.
Have the data acquisition devices publish data to Cloud Pub/Sub.
Establish a Cloud Interconnect between all remote data centers and Google.
Write a Cloud Dataflow pipeline that aggregates all data in session windows.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Pub/Sub provides managed, asynchronous event ingestion that decouples publishers from downstream processing and is designed for scalable, reliable event delivery. Publishing directly from the data-acquisition devices removes the leased-line dependency without the operational cost of self-managed Kafka clusters or the expense of Cloud Interconnect. Pub/Sub is also a documented fit for streaming data from IoT devices and sensors.

**Learn more:** [What is Pub/Sub?](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview) · [Pub/Sub: Introduction to reliability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/reliability-intro)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a BigQuery table that receives data directly from a Pub/Sub subscription. The ingested data is encrypted using a Google-managed encryption key. You must comply with a new organization policy requiring keys from a centralized Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) project to encrypt data at rest. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud KMS encryption key with Dataflow to ingest the existing Pub/Sub subscription to the existing BigQuery table.
Create a new BigQuery table by using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and migrate the data from the old BigQuery table.
Create a new Pub/Sub topic with CMEK and use the existing BigQuery table by using Google-managed encryption key.
Create a new BigQuery table and Pub/Sub topic by using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and migrate the data from the old BigQuery table.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery supports customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) from Cloud KMS for data at rest. Creating a CMEK-protected BigQuery table and migrating the old table’s data ensures the stored historical and destination data is protected by the centrally managed key; changing only the ingestion path or Pub/Sub topic does not re-encrypt the BigQuery table’s existing data.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery encryption at rest](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/encryption-at-rest) · [Copy a table with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/samples/bigquery-copy-table-cmek)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You monitor and optimize your team’s BigQuery instance. A particular daily report that uses a large `JOIN` operation is consistently slow. You want to inspect the query’s execution plan to identify potential performance bottlenecks within the `JOIN` as quickly as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Use the bg query --dry_run command to review the estimated number of bytes read and review query syntax.
Run a query on the INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS_BY_PROJECT view filtering by the job_ID and analyze total_bytes_processed.
Review the BigQuery audit logs in Cloud Logging.
Leverage BigQuery's Query History view and analyze the execution graph.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery’s query execution graph presents the execution plan as stages and exposes timing, resource-use, and step details. A `JOIN` stage can be inspected directly to identify stages that dominate execution time or resource consumption, making it the most direct way to diagnose JOIN-related bottlenecks.

**Learn more:** [Get query performance insights](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/query-insights) · [Query plan and timeline](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/query-plan-explanation)

",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Use Firebase Realtime Database for ingestion and storage, and Cloud Run functions for processing and analytics.","B":"Use Cloud Data Fusion for ingestion and transformation, and Cloud SQL for storage and analytics.","C":"Use Pub/Sub for ingestion, Dataflow with Apache Beam for processing, and BigQuery for storage and analytics.","D":"Use Cloud Storage for ingestion, Dataproc with Apache Spark for batch processing, and BigQuery for storage and analytics."},"correctAnswer":"C","explanation":"Pub/Sub provides scalable, reliable ingestion for continuous event streams. ",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Deploy small Kafka clusters in your data centers to buffer events.","B":"Have the data acquisition devices publish data to Cloud Pub/Sub.","C":"Establish a Cloud Interconnect between all remote data centers and Google.","D":"Write a Cloud Dataflow pipeline that aggregates all data in session windows."},"correctAnswer":"B","explanation":"Cloud Pub/Sub provides managed, asynchronous event ingestion that decouples publishers from downstream processing and is designed for scalable, reliable event delivery. The Development and External teams have the Project Viewer Identity and Access Management (IAM) role in a folder called Visualization. You want the Development Team to be able to read data from both Cloud Storage and BigQuery, while the External Team can read data only from BigQuery. What should you do?  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783810359078-1ki3x35r.jpg)

options.text: Remove Cloud Storage IAM permissions to the External Team on the acme-raw-data project.
Create Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) firewall rules on the acme-raw-data project that deny all ingress traffic from the External Team CIDR range.
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter containing both projects and BigQuery as a restricted API. Add the External Team users to the perimeter's Access Level.
Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter containing both projects and Cloud Storage as a restricted API. Add the Development Team users to the perimeter's Access Level.

questions.explanation:
VPC Service Controls is an additional, IAM-independent control layer that can restrict access to specifically protected Google Cloud services. Placing both projects in a perimeter that restricts Cloud Storage, and allowing only the Development Team through an access level, permits that team to access Cloud Storage while blocking the External Team's Cloud Storage requests despite its inherited IAM role. Because BigQuery is not restricted by this perimeter, both teams retain their existing IAM-based BigQuery read access.

**Learn more:** [Overview of VPC Service Controls](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview) · [Allow access to protected resources from outside a perimeter](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/use-access-levels)

Your company is migrating its 30-node Apache Hadoop cluster to the cloud. It wants to reuse Hadoop jobs it has already created and minimize cluster management as much as possible. It also needs to persist data beyond the cluster’s lifetime. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Google Cloud Dataflow job to process the data.
Create a Google Cloud Dataproc cluster that uses persistent disks for HDFS.
Create a Hadoop cluster on Google Compute Engine that uses persistent disks.
Create a Cloud Dataproc cluster that uses the Google Cloud Storage connector.
Create a Hadoop cluster on Google Compute Engine that uses Local SSD disks.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Dataproc is a fully managed service for Apache Hadoop workloads, reducing cluster-management overhead while supporting existing Hadoop jobs. Its automatically installed Cloud Storage connector exposes Cloud Storage through Hadoop-compatible paths, and data stored in Cloud Storage persists after the Dataproc cluster is shut down.

**Learn more:** [Dataproc FAQ](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/resources/faq) · [gcloud dataproc jobs submit hadoop](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/dataproc/jobs/submit/hadoop)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You currently use a SQL-based tool to visualize data stored in BigQuery. The data visualizations require outer joins and analytic functions. Visualizations must be based on data that is at least 4 hours old. Business users report that the visualizations take too long to generate. You want to improve the visualization-query performance while minimizing maintenance overhead for the data-preparation pipeline. What should you do?

options.text: Create materialized views with the allow_non_incremental_definition option set to true for the visualization queries. Specify the max_staleness parameter to 4 hours and the enable_refresh parameter to true. Reference the materialized views in the data visualization tool.
Create views for the visualization queries. Reference the views in the data visualization tool.

Create a Cloud Function instance to export the visualization query results as parquet files to a Cloud Storage bucket. Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger the Cloud Function every 4 hours. Reference the parquet files in the data visualization tool.

Create materialized views for the visualization queries. Use the incremental updates capability of BigQuery materialized views to handle changed data automatically. Reference the materialized views in the data visualization tool.

questions.explanation:
A non-incremental BigQuery materialized view supports outer joins and analytic functions when `allow_non_incremental_definition` is enabled. Its `max_staleness` setting can permit results up to four hours old, so visualization queries can use precomputed data for lower latency. Enabling refresh maintains the materialized view automatically, avoiding a separately managed export pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Create materialized views | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-create)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are moving a large number of files from a public HTTPS endpoint to Cloud Storage. The files are safeguarded from unauthorized access by using signed URLs. You created a TSV file containing the object-URL list and started a transfer job using Storage Transfer Service. You observe that the job ran for a long time and ultimately failed. The transfer-job logs show that it was running successfully until a certain point, after which it failed with HTTP 403 errors for the remaining files. You confirmed that the source system had not changed. You need to resolve the issue so that you can resume the migration process. What should you do?

options.text: Set up Cloud Storage FUSE, and mount the Cloud Storage bucket on a Compute Engine instance. Remove the completed files from the TSV file. Use a shell script to iterate through the TSV file and download the remaining URLs to the FUSE mount point.
Renew the TLS certificate of the HTTPS endpoint. Remove the completed files from the TSV file and rerun the Storage Transfer Service job.

Create a new TSV file for the remaining files by generating signed URLs with a longer validity period. Split the TSV file into multiple smaller files and submit them as separate Storage Transfer Service jobs in parallel.
Update the file checksums in the TSV file from using MD5 to SHA256. Remove the completed files from the TSV file and rerun the Storage Transfer Service job.

questions.explanation:
Signed URLs grant access only until their configured expiration time. A long-running transfer can therefore receive HTTP 403 responses for objects whose signed URLs expire before Storage Transfer Service fetches them. Regenerating signed URLs with a longer validity period for the remaining objects restores authorization, and splitting the work into smaller parallel jobs shortens the time before each URL is used.

**Learn more:** [Transfer from public URLs to Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/create-url-list) · [Sources and sinks for Storage Transfer Service](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/sources-and-sinks)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to orchestrate a pipeline across several Google Cloud services: a batch Dataflow job, followed by a BigQuery query job and then a Vertex AI batch prediction. Select Compute Engine with cron.
Select Dataproc with Apache Oozie.
Select Cloud Workflows.

Cloud Workflows is a fully managed, serverless service for executing Google Cloud services in an explicitly defined order. Its connectors support Dataflow jobs, BigQuery, and Vertex AI, making it suitable for a sequential cross-service pipeline without managing orchestration infrastructure.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to create a SQL pipeline. You must configure the pipeline to retry when errors occur. You want it to send an email notification after three consecutive failures. What should you do?

options.text: Use the BigQueryUpsertTableOperator in Cloud Composer, set the retry parameter to three, and set the email_on_failure parameter to true.
Use the BigQueryInsertJobOperator in Cloud Composer, set the retry parameter to three, and set the email_on_failure parameter to true.
Create a BigQuery scheduled query to run the SQL transformation with schedule options that repeats every two hours, and enable email notifications.

Create a BigQuery scheduled query to run the SQL transformation with schedule options that repeats every two hours, and enable notification to Pub/Sub topic. Use Pub/Sub and Cloud Functions to send an email after three failed executions.

`BigQueryInsertJobOperator` submits the BigQuery SQL job that performs the transformation and can write results to an existing destination table. Cloud Composer/Airflow task settings support retries and `email_on_failure`; the email is sent when the operator reaches its final failed state after retries are exhausted. questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team has created multiple BigQuery curated datasets that contain anonymized industry benchmark data. What should you do?

options.text: Publish the datasets as listings within BigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub).
Export the datasets to partner-specific Cloud Storage buckets.
Create authorized views for each dataset and grant access to each partner.
Grant the roles/bigquery.dataViewer IAM role to the partner group email addresses on the datasets.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery sharing (formerly Analytics Hub) uses publishable listings to securely share BigQuery datasets across organizational boundaries at scale. Partners can discover and subscribe to a listing, creating a linked dataset in their own Google Cloud project for read-only querying without replicating the shared data.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You administer a BigQuery dataset that uses a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK). You must share the dataset with a partner organization that lacks access to your CMEK. What should you do?

Export the tables to parquet files to a Cloud Storage bucket and grant the storageinsights.viewer role on the bucket to the partner organization.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a data model in BigQuery to store retail transaction data. Your two largest tables, `sales_transaction_header` and `sales_transaction_line`, have a tightly coupled, immutable relationship. These tables are seldom changed after loading and are often joined in queries. You need to model the `sales_transaction_header` and `sales_transaction_line` tables to enhance the performance of data analytics queries. What should you do?

options.text: Create a sales_transaction table that holds the sales_transaction_header information as rows and the sales_transaction_line rows as nested and repeated fields.
Create a sales_transaction table that holds the sales_transaction_header and sales_transaction_line information as rows, duplicating the sales_transaction_header data for each line.
Create a sales_transaction table that stores the sales_transaction_header and sales_transaction_line data as a JSON data type.
Create separate sales_transaction_header and sales_transaction_line tables and, when querying, specify the sales_transaction_line first in the WHERE clause.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery recommends denormalizing hierarchical parent-child data that is frequently queried together by storing the parent as one row and the child records as nested, repeated fields. This preserves the one-to-many transaction-header-to-line relationship while avoiding the communication and shuffle overhead of frequent joins.

**Learn more:** [Use nested and repeated fields — BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/best-practices-performance-nested) · [Specify nested and repeated columns in table schemas — BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/nested-repeated)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a BigQuery dataset called `customers`. All tables will be tagged using a Data Catalog tag template named `gdpr`. The template includes one mandatory Boolean field, `has_sensitive_data`.  
  
All employees must be able to perform a simple search to locate tables in the dataset where `has_sensitive_data` is either `true` or `false`. However, only the Human Resources (HR) group must be able to view the data in tables where `has_sensitive_data` is `true`. You grant the all-employees group the `bigquery.metadataViewer` and `bigquery.connectionUser` roles on the dataset. You want to minimize configuration overhead. What should you do next?

options.text: Create the “gdpr” tag template with private visibility. Assign the bigquery.dataViewer role to the HR group on the tables that contain sensitive data.

Create the “gdpr” tag template with private visibility. Assign the datacatalog.tagTemplateViewer role on this tag to the all employees group, and assign the bigquery.dataViewer role to the HR group on the tables that contain sensitive data.
Create the “gdpr” tag template with public visibility. Assign the bigquery.dataViewer role to the HR group on the tables that contain sensitive data.

Create the “gdpr” tag template with public visibility. Assign the datacatalog.tagTemplateViewer role on this tag to the all employees group, and assign the bigquery.dataViewer role to the HR group on the tables that contain sensitive data.

questions.explanation:
Public Data Catalog tags can be found by tag value with a simple search query and do not require separate tag-template access to appear with assets the user can view. The `bigquery.metadataViewer` role permits table metadata discovery but not table-data reads, while `bigquery.dataViewer` granted on individual tables permits reading those tables. questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You recently deployed several data-processing jobs in your Cloud Composer 2 environment. Some Apache Airflow tasks are failing. The monitoring dashboard shows increased total worker memory usage and worker pod evictions. You need to resolve these errors. What should you do? (Choose two.)

options.text: Increase the directed acyclic graph (DAG) file parsing interval.

Increase the maximum number of workers and reduce worker concurrency.
Increase the memory available to the Airflow workers.
Increase the memory available to the Airflow triggerer.

questions.explanation:
Worker pod evictions commonly result from out-of-memory conditions. Reducing worker concurrency lowers the number of tasks handled simultaneously by each worker, giving each task more memory; increasing the maximum number of workers can maintain overall task capacity. Increasing the memory allocated to Airflow workers directly raises the resource limit that is causing the evictions.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You run an IoT pipeline based on Apache Kafka that typically receives about 5000 messages per second. You want to use Google Cloud Platform to create an alert as soon as the 1-hour moving average falls below 4000 messages per second. What should you do?

options.text: Consume the stream of data in Dataflow using Kafka IO. Set a sliding time window of 1 hour every 5 minutes. Compute the average when the window closes, and send an alert if the average is less than 4000 messages.
Consume the stream of data in Dataflow using Kafka IO. Set a fixed time window of 1 hour. Compute the average when the window closes, and send an alert if the average is less than 4000 messages.

Use Kafka Connect to link your Kafka message queue to Pub/Sub. Use a Dataflow template to write your messages from Pub/Sub to Bigtable. Use Cloud Scheduler to run a script every hour that counts the number of rows created in Bigtable in the last hour. If that number falls below 4000, send an alert.

Use Kafka Connect to link your Kafka message queue to Pub/Sub. Use a Dataflow template to write your messages from Pub/Sub to BigQuery. Use Cloud Scheduler to run a script every five minutes that counts the number of rows created in BigQuery in the last hour. If that number falls below 4000, send an alert.

questions.explanation:
A 1-hour sliding (hopping) window evaluated every 5 minutes creates overlapping windows, each containing the most recent hour of messages, so it can calculate and alert on a current 1-hour moving average at five-minute intervals. Google Cloud documents that hopping windows overlap and are used for running averages; fixed windows are disjoint intervals.

**Learn more:** [Streaming pipelines](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-pipelines)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to migrate 1 PB of data from an on-premises data center to Google Cloud. questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are defining a data-governance strategy for a new BigQuery table containing medical and financial data. questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are monitoring your organization’s data lake, which is hosted on BigQuery. You are planning to use Cloud Storage as part of a data lake solution. The Cloud Storage bucket will hold objects ingested from external systems. Each object will be ingested once, and individual-object access patterns will be random. You want to minimize the cost of storing and retrieving these objects while ensuring that any cost-optimization measures are transparent to users and applications. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Storage bucket with Autoclass enabled.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket with an Object Lifecycle Management policy to transition objects from Standard to Coldline storage class if an object age reaches 30 days.
Create a Cloud Storage bucket with an Object Lifecycle Management policy to transition objects from Standard to Coldline storage class if an object is not live.

Create two Cloud Storage buckets. Use the Standard storage class for the first bucket, and use the Coldline storage class for the second bucket. Migrate objects from the first bucket to the second bucket after 30 days.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage Autoclass automatically selects and transitions storage classes according to each object's access pattern, making it suitable for unknown or unpredictable access. It manages those transitions without application changes and Autoclass-managed objects do not incur retrieval fees, avoiding the retrieval-cost risk of placing randomly accessed objects in Coldline through a fixed lifecycle rule.

**Learn more:** [Autoclass | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/autoclass) · [Storage pricing | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],A shipping company has live package-tracking data that is sent to an Apache Kafka stream in real time and then loaded into BigQuery. Analysts at your company want to query the tracking data in BigQuery to analyze geospatial trends throughout a package’s lifecycle. The table was initially created with ingest-date partitioning. Over time, query processing time has increased. You need to implement a change that improves query performance in BigQuery. What should you do?

options.text: Implement clustering in BigQuery on the ingest date column.
Implement clustering in BigQuery on the package-tracking ID column.
Tier older data onto Cloud Storage files and create a BigQuery table using Cloud Storage as an external data source.
Re-create the table using data partitioning on the package delivery date.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery clustering sorts storage blocks by the clustering column. Clustering the existing ingestion-time-partitioned table by package-tracking ID colocates a package’s tracking events and lets BigQuery prune irrelevant blocks when queries filter by that ID, reducing data scanned for lifecycle analysis. [Introduction to clustered tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/clustered-tables)

**Learn more:** [Introduction to clustered tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/clustered-tables) · [Introduction to partitioned tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have designed an Apache Beam processing pipeline that reads from a Pub/Sub topic. The topic has a one-day message-retention duration and writes to a Cloud Storage bucket. You must choose a bucket location and processing strategy that prevent data loss during a regional outage with an RPO of 15 minutes. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Use a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. Seek the subscription back in time by 15 minutes to recover the acknowledged messages.4. Start the Dataflow job in a secondary region.

1. Use a multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. Seek the subscription back in time by 60 minutes to recover the acknowledged messages.4. Start the Dataflow job in a secondary region.

1. Use a regional Cloud Storage bucket.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. Seek the subscription back in time by one day to recover the acknowledged messages.4. Start the Dataflow job in a secondary region and write in a bucket in the same region.

1. Use a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket with turbo replication enabled.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. Seek the subscription back in time by 60 minutes to recover the acknowledged messages.4. Start the Dataflow job in a secondary region.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage turbo replication is available only for dual-region buckets and is designed to replicate newly written objects to both regions within a 15-minute RPO. Default replication has a 12-hour RPO, so neither a standard dual- or multi-region bucket nor a regional bucket satisfies the requirement. Pub/Sub topic retention permits replay of retained acknowledged messages, enabling a secondary-region Dataflow job to reprocess an overlap after failover.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage data availability and durability](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/availability-durability) · [Replay and purge messages with seek](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/replay-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for an advertising company and have developed a Spark ML model that predicts click-through rates for advertisement blocks. All development has been done in your on-premises data center, but the company is now migrating to Google Cloud. Because the data center will close soon, a rapid lift-and-shift migration is required. However, the data you have used will be migrated to BigQuery. You periodically retrain the Spark ML models, so the existing training pipelines must be moved to Google Cloud. What should you do?

options.text: Use Vertex AI for training existing Spark ML models
Rewrite your models on TensorFlow, and start using Vertex AI
Use Dataproc for training existing Spark ML models, but start reading data directly from BigQuery
Spin up a Spark cluster on Compute Engine, and train Spark ML models on the data exported from BigQuery

questions.explanation:
Dataproc provides managed Apache Spark and can run existing Spark ML training pipelines without rewriting the models. The Spark BigQuery connector enables those workloads to read the migrated training data directly from BigQuery, which supports a rapid lift-and-shift migration.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery connector code samples | Dataproc](https://cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/examples/bigquery-example) · [Use Dataproc, BigQuery, and Apache Spark ML for machine learning](https://cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/tutorials/bigquery-sparkml)

",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Create a Cloud Storage bucket with Autoclass enabled.","B":"Create a Cloud Storage bucket with an Object Lifecycle Management policy to transition objects from Standard to Coldline storage class if an object age reaches 30 days.","C":"Create a Cloud Storage bucket with an Object Lifecycle Management policy to transition objects from Standard to Coldline storage class if an object is not live.","D":"Create two Cloud Storage buckets. Use the Standard storage class for the first bucket, and use the Coldline storage class for the second bucket. Migrate objects from the first bucket to the second bucket after 30 days."},"correctAnswer":"A","explanation":"Cloud Storage Autoclass automatically selects and transitions storage classes according to each object's access pattern, making it suitable for unknown or unpredictable access. It manages those transitions without application changes and Autoclass-managed objects do not incur retrieval fees, avoiding the retrieval-cost risk of placing randomly accessed objects in Coldline through a fixed lifecycle rule.

**Learn more:** [Autoclass | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/autoclass) · [Storage pricing | Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/storage/pricing)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"1f547e3b-6cb5-490c-81b3-e05d76018b07","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-data-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]
51:[["$","p",null,{"children":"A shipping company has live package-tracking data that is sent to an Apache Kafka stream in real time and then loaded into BigQuery. Analysts at your company want to query the tracking data in BigQuery to analyze geospatial trends throughout a package’s lifecycle. The table was initially created with ingest-date partitioning. Over time, query processing time has increased. You need to implement a change that improves query performance in BigQuery. What should you do?"}],"
",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"Implement clustering in BigQuery on the ingest date column.","B":"Implement clustering in BigQuery on the package-tracking ID column.","C":"Tier older data onto Cloud Storage files and create a BigQuery table using Cloud Storage as an external data source.","D":"Re-create the table using data partitioning on the package delivery date."},"correctAnswer":"B","explanation":"BigQuery clustering sorts storage blocks by the clustering column. Clustering the existing ingestion-time-partitioned table by package-tracking ID colocates a package’s tracking events and lets BigQuery prune irrelevant blocks when queries filter by that ID, reducing data scanned for lifecycle analysis. [Introduction to clustered tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/clustered-tables)

**Learn more:** [Introduction to clustered tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/clustered-tables) · [Introduction to partitioned tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables)","trackingInfo":{"questionId":"71f05e2f-00ac-42ac-833b-4dbd548f5a8c","examProvider":"google","examName":"professional-data-engineer","mode":"default"}}]]

",["$","$L54",null,{"choices":{"A":"1. Use a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. Start the Dataflow job in a secondary region.","C":"1. Use a regional Cloud Storage bucket.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. Seek the subscription back in time by one day to recover the acknowledged messages.4. Start the Dataflow job in a secondary region and write in a bucket in the same region.","D":"1. Use a dual-region Cloud Storage bucket with turbo replication enabled.2. Monitor Dataflow metrics with Cloud Monitoring to determine when an outage occurs.3. You operate a data-processing application on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Containers must launch using their latest available configurations from a container registry. Your GKE nodes require GPUs, local SSDs, and 8 Gbps of bandwidth. You want to provision the data-processing infrastructure efficiently and manage the deployment process. What should you do?

options.text: Use Compute Engine startup scripts to pull container images, and use gcloud commands to provision the infrastructure.
Use Cloud Build to schedule a job using Terraform build to provision the infrastructure and launch with the most current container images.
Use GKE to autoscale containers, and use gcloud commands to provision the infrastructure.
Use Dataflow to provision the data pipeline, and use Cloud Scheduler to run the job.

questions.explanation:
Terraform defines and provisions GKE infrastructure declaratively, including the node configuration required for the workload, and maintains its state for repeatable updates. Cloud Build can automate the build and deployment workflow and deploy a specified current container image to GKE, making it the appropriate infrastructure-as-code and deployment combination.

A data analyst on your team needs to analyze data using BigQuery. The analyst wants to create a data pipeline that loads 200 CSV files, averaging 15 MB each, from a Cloud Storage bucket into BigQuery every day. The data must be ingested and transformed before it is available for analysis in BigQuery. You need to recommend a fully managed, no-code solution for the analyst. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Run function and schedule it to run daily using Cloud Scheduler to load the data into BigQuery.
Use the BigQuery Data Transfer Service to load files from Cloud Storage to BigQuery, create a BigQuery job which transforms the data using BigQuery SQL and schedule it to run daily.
Build a custom Apache Beam pipeline and run it on Dataflow to load the file from Cloud Storage to BigQuery and schedule it to run daily using Cloud Composer.
Create a pipeline by using BigQuery pipelines and schedule it to load the data into BigQuery daily.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery pipelines provide a fully managed scheduled workflow that can include a data-preparation task. BigQuery data preparation supports loading files from Cloud Storage and applying visual cleansing and transformation steps before writing the resulting table for analysis. This keeps ingestion and transformation in one scheduled no-code workflow. BigQuery Data Transfer Service supports the CSV load, but a separate BigQuery SQL job requires writing and maintaining SQL rather than using a no-code pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to BigQuery pipelines](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/workflows-introduction) · [Prepare data with Gemini](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/data-prep-get-suggestions)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s customer and order databases are frequently under heavy load, making it difficult to perform analytics on them without affecting operations.  
  
The databases run in a MySQL cluster, with nightly backups created by using `mysqldump`. You want to run analytics with minimal operational impact. What should you do?

options.text: Add a node to the MySQL cluster and build an OLAP cube there.
Use an ETL tool to load the data from MySQL into Google BigQuery.
Connect an on-premises Apache Hadoop cluster to MySQL and perform ETL.
Mount the backups to Google Cloud SQL, and then process the data using Google Cloud Dataproc.

questions.explanation:
Loading MySQL data into BigQuery through ETL separates analytical workloads from the transactional MySQL cluster. BigQuery is a managed analytical platform whose compute and storage architecture is designed to scale analytics independently, avoiding resource contention with operational database workloads.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/introduction?hl=en) · [Datastream for BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/datastream-for-bigquery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are analyzing a company’s stock price. Every 5 seconds, you must calculate a moving average for the prior 30 seconds of data. You read data from Pub/Sub and use Dataflow to perform the analysis. How should you configure the windowed pipeline?

options.text: Use a fixed window with a duration of 5 seconds. Emit results by setting the following trigger: AfterProcessingTime.pastFirstElementInPane().plusDelayOf (Duration.standardSeconds(30))
Use a fixed window with a duration of 30 seconds. Emit results by setting the following trigger: AfterWatermark.pastEndOfWindow().plusDelayOf (Duration.standardSeconds(5))
Use a sliding window with a duration of 5 seconds. Emit results by setting the following trigger: AfterProcessingTime.pastFirstElementInPane().plusDelayOf (Duration.standardSeconds(30))
Use a sliding window with a duration of 30 seconds and a period of 5 seconds. Emit results by setting the following trigger: AfterWatermark.pastEndOfWindow ()

questions.explanation:
A 30-second sliding window that advances every 5 seconds creates overlapping 30-second intervals, yielding a moving average at five-second intervals. `AfterWatermark.pastEndOfWindow()` fires when the watermark passes the window’s end, producing the result for each event-time window. Apache Beam documents sliding windows as overlapping fixed-width time intervals and documents `AfterWatermark.pastEndOfWindow()` as firing when the watermark passes the end of the window.

**Learn more:** [Apache Beam Programming Guide](https://beam.apache.org/documentation/programming-guide/) · [Apache Beam AfterWatermark API](https://beam.apache.org/releases/javadoc/current/org/apache/beam/sdk/transforms/windowing/AfterWatermark.html)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to load some existing on-premises data into BigQuery on Google Cloud. Depending on the use case, you want to stream or batch-load the data. You also want to mask sensitive data before it is loaded into BigQuery. You must accomplish this programmatically while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Data Fusion to design your pipeline, use the Cloud DLP plug-in to de-identify data within your pipeline, and then move the data into BigQuery.

Use the BigQuery Data Transfer Service to schedule your migration. After the data is populated in BigQuery, use the connection to the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) API to de-identify the necessary data.

Create your pipeline with Dataflow through the Apache Beam SDK for Python, customizing separate options within your code for streaming, batch processing, and Cloud DLP. Select BigQuery as your data sink.
Set up Datastream to replicate your on-premise data on BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Dataflow, using the Apache Beam SDK for Python, supports both batch and streaming pipelines in code and can write to BigQuery. The pipeline can call Cloud DLP (Sensitive Data Protection) to de-identify data before it reaches the BigQuery sink, satisfying the requirement to mask sensitive data before loading while avoiding the persistent Cloud Data Fusion instance costs.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/overview) · [Data Masking/Tokenization from Cloud Storage to BigQuery (using Cloud DLP) template](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/templates/provided/dlp-text-to-bigquery?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your data science team must run interactive SQL queries on large datasets in Apache Parquet format that are stored in a Cloud Storage bucket. The team knows Apache Hive and wants to use its existing HiveQL queries.  
  
You need to provide an environment where the team can execute interactive HiveQL queries directly against the Cloud Storage data while keeping operational overhead to a minimum. What should you do?

options.text: Install and configure an Apache Hadoop and Hive cluster manually on a group of Compute Engine instances.
Load the Parquet data into a BigQuery native table and use the BigQuery Connector for Hive to run the queries.
Configure BigQuery with an external table definition pointing to the Parquet files.
Deploy a Dataproc cluster with Hive services enabled.

questions.explanation:
Dataproc is a managed Hadoop ecosystem service that includes Apache Hive and integrates with Cloud Storage through its installed Cloud Storage connector. It can run Hive queries, including HiveQL that defines external tables located in `gs://` paths, while Google manages cluster provisioning and operation. BigQuery external tables can read Parquet files in Cloud Storage, but they are queried with GoogleSQL rather than HiveQL.

**Learn more:** [Dataproc FAQ](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/resources/faq) · [Submit a Hive job to a Dataproc cluster](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sdk/gcloud/reference/dataproc/jobs/submit/hive)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You created an analytics environment on Google Cloud so your data scientist team can explore data without affecting the on-premises Apache Hadoop solution. Data in the on-premises Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) cluster is stored in Optimized Row Columnar (ORC) formatted files with multiple columns of Hive partitioning. The data scientist team must be able to explore the data in a way similar to how they used the on-premises HDFS cluster with SQL on the Hive query engine. You need to select the most cost-effective storage and processing solution. What should you do?

options.text: Import the ORC files to Bigtable tables for the data scientist team.
Import the ORC files to BigQuery tables for the data scientist team.
Copy the ORC files on Cloud Storage, then deploy a Dataproc cluster for the data scientist team.
Copy the ORC files on Cloud Storage, then create external BigQuery tables for the data scientist team.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage can act as durable storage that is compatible with Hadoop-style access through Dataproc’s automatically installed HDFS-compatible Cloud Storage connector. A Dataproc cluster supplies the Hadoop/Hive environment, allowing the existing ORC files and Hive partition layout to be queried with Hive SQL while keeping persistent data separate from transient cluster storage.

**Learn more:** [Dataproc FAQ](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/resources/faq) · [Enable Hive data lineage in Dataproc](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataproc/docs/guides/hive-lineage)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has expanded rapidly and is now ingesting data at a substantially higher rate than before. You manage the daily batch MapReduce analytics jobs in Apache Hadoop. However, the recent data increase has caused the batch jobs to fall behind. You have been asked to recommend ways the development team can improve analytics responsiveness without increasing costs. What should you recommend?

options.text: Rewrite the job in Pig.
Rewrite the job in Apache Spark.
Increase the size of the Hadoop cluster.
Decrease the size of the Hadoop cluster but also rewrite the job in Hive.

questions.explanation:
Apache Spark is a fast processing engine that is compatible with Hadoop data and can run on Hadoop clusters. Rewriting batch analytics in Spark can improve responsiveness without purchasing additional cluster capacity; expanding the Hadoop cluster would increase costs. Spark documentation reports faster performance than Hadoop MapReduce for comparable large-scale processing workloads.

**Learn more:** [Apache Spark FAQ](https://spark.apache.org/faq.html)

A data scientist has built a BigQuery ML model and asks you to build an ML pipeline for serving predictions. You have a REST API application that must return predictions for an individual user ID with latency below 100 milliseconds. You use this query to generate predictions:  
  
```sql  
SELECT predicted_label, user_id  
FROM ML.PREDICT (MODEL 'dataset.model', table user_features)  
```  
  
How should you create the ML pipeline?

options.text: Add a WHERE clause to the query, and grant the BigQuery Data Viewer role to the application service account.
Create an Authorized View with the provided query. Share the dataset that contains the view with the application service account.
Create a Dataflow pipeline using BigQueryIO to read results from the query. Grant the Dataflow Worker role to the application service account.

Create a Dataflow pipeline using BigQueryIO to read predictions for all users from the query. Write the results to Bigtable using BigtableIO. Grant the Bigtable Reader role to the application service account so that the application can read predictions for individual users from Bigtable.

questions.explanation:
`ML.PREDICT` produces one output row for each input row and is suited to generating a set of predictions. For a user-facing, low-latency serving path, predictions can be generated in batch, written to Bigtable with `user_id` as the lookup key, and read directly by the REST application. Bigtable is designed for large-scale, low-latency application serving, while BigQuery is primarily an analytic and batch-inference system.

**Learn more:** [The ML.PREDICT function](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/bigqueryml-syntax-predict) · [Bigtable vs. BigQuery: What’s the difference?](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/bigtable-vs-bigquery-whats-difference)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a shipping company that uses handheld scanners to scan shipping labels. The company has strict data-privacy standards requiring scanners to transmit only tracking numbers when events are sent to Kafka topics. A recent software update caused the scanners to inadvertently send recipients’ personally identifiable information (PII) to analytics systems, violating user privacy rules. You need to rapidly create a scalable solution with cloud-native managed services to stop PII exposure to the analytics systems. What should you do?

options.text: Create an authorized view in BigQuery to restrict access to tables with sensitive data.
Install a third-party data validation tool on Compute Engine virtual machines to check the incoming data for sensitive information.
Use Cloud Logging to analyze the data passed through the total pipeline to identify transactions that may contain sensitive information.

Build a Cloud Function that reads the topics and makes a call to the Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) API. Use the tagging and confidence levels to either pass or quarantine the data in a bucket for review.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Sensitive Data Protection) can synchronously inspect event content for configured PII information types and return findings with likelihood levels. A Cloud Function can process Kafka-topic events, forward events containing only permitted tracking data, and quarantine events with detected PII for review before they reach analytics systems.

**Learn more:** [Sensitive Data Protection overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/concepts) · [Inspecting text for sensitive data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/inspecting-text)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You store and analyze relational data in BigQuery on Google Cloud, with all data located in US regions. You also have a variety of object stores across Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services (AWS), likewise in US regions. You want to query all of your data in BigQuery each day while moving as little data as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Use BigQuery Data Transfer Service to load files from Azure and AWS into BigQuery.
Create a Dataflow pipeline to ingest files from Azure and AWS to BigQuery.
Load files from AWS and Azure to Cloud Storage with Cloud Shell gsutil rsync arguments.
Use the BigQuery Omni functionality and BigLake tables to query files in Azure and AWS.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery Omni lets BigQuery analyze data that remains in Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage through BigLake tables. BigQuery Omni joins support combining those external tables with BigQuery tables in the US multi-region, eliminating the need to copy the source data into BigQuery before querying it.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to BigQuery Omni](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/omni-introduction) · [Introduction to BigLake tables](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/biglake-intro)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a query that filters a BigQuery table with a `WHERE` clause on timestamp and ID columns. By using `bq query "-dry_run"`, you learn that the query causes a full table scan, although the timestamp and ID filters select only a tiny fraction of the total data. You want to reduce the amount of data BigQuery scans with minimal changes to the existing SQL queries. What should you do?

options.text: Create a separate table for each ID.
Use the LIMIT keyword to reduce the number of rows returned.
Recreate the table with a partitioning column and clustering column.
Use the bq query --maximum_bytes_billed flag to restrict the number of bytes billed.

questions.explanation:
Partitioning the table by the timestamp column enables partition pruning for timestamp filters, and clustering by ID enables block pruning for ID filters within those partitions. Together, these table properties reduce the bytes BigQuery scans while allowing the existing `WHERE` filters to remain essentially unchanged.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to partitioned tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables) · [Introduction to clustered tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/clustered-tables)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are operating a Dataflow pipeline that receives messages from a Pub/Sub topic and writes results to a BigQuery dataset in the EU. The pipeline currently runs in `europe-west4` with a maximum of 3 `n1-standard-1` workers.  
  
During peak periods, the pipeline struggles to process records promptly while all 3 workers have maximum CPU utilization. Which two actions can you take to improve pipeline performance? (Choose two.)

options.text: Increase the number of max workers
Use a larger instance type for your Dataflow workers
Change the zone of your Dataflow pipeline to run in us-central1

Create a temporary table in Bigtable that will act as a buffer for new data. Create a new step in your pipeline to write to this table first, and then create a new pipeline to write from Bigtable to BigQuery

Create a temporary table in Cloud Spanner that will act as a buffer for new data. Create a new step in your pipeline to write to this table first, and then create a new pipeline to write from Cloud Spanner to BigQuery

questions.explanation:
Dataflow horizontal autoscaling can add worker instances up to the configured maximum, increasing parallel processing capacity. Configuring a larger Dataflow worker machine type increases the compute resources available to each worker. These directly address CPU saturation in the worker pool.

**Learn more:** [Horizontal Autoscaling | Cloud Dataflow](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/horizontal-autoscaling) · [Configure Dataflow worker VMs | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/configure-worker-vm)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],An online brokerage firm needs an architecture to process a high volume of trades. Create a secure queuing system that triggers jobs. The jobs will run in Google Cloud and invoke the company’s Python API to execute trades. You need to implement the solution efficiently. What should you do?

options.text: Use a Pub/Sub push subscription to trigger a Cloud Function to pass the data to the Python API.
Write an application hosted on a Compute Engine instance that makes a push subscription to the Pub/Sub topic.
Write an application that makes a queue in a NoSQL database.
Use Cloud Composer to subscribe to a Pub/Sub topic and call the Python API.

questions.explanation:
A Pub/Sub push subscription can deliver messages to a Cloud Function, providing a managed, scalable event-driven queue and compute path. The function can process the trade job and invoke the Python API, while authenticated Pub/Sub push delivery supports secure invocation without operating queue or VM infrastructure.

**Learn more:** [Push subscriptions | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/push) · [Configure a Cloud Run functions trigger with Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/use-with-cloud-function-triggers)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You receive CSV data files every month from a third party. You need to cleanse this data, but the file schema changes every third month. Your requirements for implementing these transformations include:  
  
- Running the transformations on a schedule  
- Allowing non-developer analysts to modify transformations  
- Supplying a graphical tool to design transformations  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Use Dataprep by Trifacta to build and maintain the transformation recipes, and execute them on a scheduled basis
Load each month's CSV data into BigQuery, and write a SQL query to transform the data to a standard schema. Merge the transformed tables together with a SQL query
Help the analysts write a Dataflow pipeline in Python to perform the transformation. The Python code should be stored in a revision control system and modified as the incoming data's schema changes

Use Apache Spark on Dataproc to infer the schema of the CSV file before creating a Dataframe. Then implement the transformations in Spark SQL before writing the data out to Cloud Storage and loading into BigQuery

questions.explanation:
Dataprep by Trifacta supports visual, no-code creation and maintenance of reusable transformation recipes, enabling analysts to adapt recipes when source schemas change. Its flows can also be scheduled for recurring execution, satisfying both the operational scheduling and analyst-friendly graphical design requirements.

**Learn more:** [New flexibility: Run your Dataprep jobs with BigQuery or Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/introducing-dataprep-bigquery-pushdown) · [Scheduling and sampling arrive for Google Cloud Dataprep](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/scheduling-and-sampling-arrive-for-google-cloud-dataprep)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are integrating an internal IT application with Google BigQuery so that users can query BigQuery through the application's interface. You do not want individual users to authenticate with BigQuery, and you do not want to grant them access to the dataset. You need to securely access BigQuery from your IT application. What should you do?

options.text: Create groups for your users and give those groups access to the dataset
Integrate with a single sign-on (SSO) platform, and pass each user's credentials along with the query request
Create a service account and grant dataset access to that account. Use the service account's private key to access the dataset
Create a dummy user and grant dataset access to that user. Store the username and password for that user in a file on the files system, and use those credentials to access the BigQuery dataset

questions.explanation:
A service account is a non-human identity for an application. Granting the service account the required dataset permissions allows the application to query BigQuery using that identity, without granting BigQuery access to, or requiring BigQuery authentication from, individual application users.

**Learn more:** [Get started with authentication | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/authentication/getting-started) · [Control access to resources with IAM | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/control-access-to-resources-iam)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has hired a new data scientist who wants to conduct complex analyses across very large datasets stored in Google Cloud Storage and in a Cassandra cluster on Google Compute Engine. The scientist mainly wants to create labelled datasets for machine learning projects, together with some visualization work. She says her laptop lacks the power to perform these tasks and that this is slowing her down. You want to help her complete her work.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Run a local version of Jupiter on the laptop.
Grant the user access to Google Cloud Shell.
Host a visualization tool on a VM on Google Compute Engine.
Deploy Google Cloud Datalab to a virtual machine (VM) on Google Compute Engine.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Datalab provides a Jupyter-based environment for data exploration, analysis, and visualization, and deploying it on a Compute Engine VM supplies scalable cloud compute instead of relying on the data scientist’s underpowered laptop. It is suited to working with Google Cloud Storage while supporting the broader interactive analysis and visualization workflow.

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud Platform for data scientists: using Jupyter Notebooks with Apache Spark on Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/google-cloud-platform-for-data-scientists-using-jupyter-notebooks-with-apache-spark-on-google-cloud)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You launched a new gaming app nearly three years ago. You have uploaded the previous day’s log files to separate Google BigQuery tables named in the format `LOGS_yyyymmdd`. You have used table wildcard functions to create daily and monthly reports across all time ranges. Recently, you found that some queries spanning long date ranges exceed the 1,000-table limit and fail. How can you resolve this issue?

options.text: Convert all daily log tables into date-partitioned tables
Convert the sharded tables into a single partitioned table
Enable query caching so you can cache data from previous months
Create separate views to cover each month, and query from these views

questions.explanation:
BigQuery recommends partitioning rather than date sharding. A single partitioned table stores the daily data as partitions, so date-range queries can prune the relevant partitions without referencing more than 1,000 separate sharded tables.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to partitioned tables | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables) · [Query multiple tables using a wildcard table | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-wildcard-tables)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You intend to deploy Cloud SQL with MySQL. You must ensure high availability if a zone fails. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud SQL instance in one zone, and create a failover replica in another zone within the same region.
Create a Cloud SQL instance in one zone, and create a read replica in another zone within the same region.
Create a Cloud SQL instance in one zone, and configure an external read replica in a zone in a different region.
Create a Cloud SQL instance in a region, and configure automatic backup to a Cloud Storage bucket in the same region.

questions.explanation:
Cloud SQL high availability uses a primary and a secondary-zone standby within the same region, with automatic failover when the primary instance or its zone fails. For legacy MySQL HA terminology, this standby is called a failover replica. Read replicas do not provide the automatic failover capability required for zonal high availability.

**Learn more:** [About high availability | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/high-availability) · [About replication in Cloud SQL | Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a data-processing pipeline. The pipeline must automatically scale as load grows. Messages must be processed at least once and be ordered within 1-hour windows. How should you design the solution?

options.text: Use Apache Kafka for message ingestion and use Cloud Dataproc for streaming analysis.
Use Apache Kafka for message ingestion and use Cloud Dataflow for streaming analysis.
Use Cloud Pub/Sub for message ingestion and Cloud Dataproc for streaming analysis.
Use Cloud Pub/Sub for message ingestion and Cloud Dataflow for streaming analysis.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Pub/Sub provides at-least-once message delivery and can preserve order for related messages by using ordering keys. Cloud Dataflow is managed streaming processing that autoscales workers and supports windowing unbounded data into timestamp-based windows, including fixed one-hour windows.

**Learn more:** [Order messages | Pub/Sub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/ordering) · [Dataflow overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/overview)

questions.domain: Preparing and using data for analysis

options.text: Provide the data science team access to Dataflow to create a pipeline to prepare and validate the raw data and load data into BigQuery for data exploration.
Create an external table in BigQuery and use SQL to transform the data as necessary. Provide the data science team access to the external tables to explore the raw data.
Load the data into BigQuery and use SQL to transform the data as necessary. Provide the data science team access to staging tables to explore the raw data.
Provide the data science team access to Dataprep to prepare, validate, and explore the data within Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Dataprep provides a graphical, low-code interface for visually exploring, cleaning, preparing, and validating data, with integration for reading raw data from Cloud Storage. This fits a data science team that needs to profile and cleanse stored files without building Dataflow pipelines or writing BigQuery SQL.

**Learn more:** [Improving data quality for machine learning and analytics with Cloud Dataprep](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/improving-data-quality-for-machine-learning-and-analytics-with-cloud-dataprep) · [Google Cloud Platform adds new tools for easy data preparation and integration](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/google-cloud-platform-adds-new-tools-for-easy-data-preparation-and-integration)

You collect IoT sensor data from millions of devices worldwide and store it in BigQuery. Your access pattern uses recent data filtered by `location_id` and `device_version`, using the following query:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783859953172-r5nlddam.png)  
  
You want to optimize query cost and performance. How should you organize your data?

options.text: Partition table data by create_date, location_id, and device_version.
Partition table data by create_date, cluster table data by location_id, and device_version.
Cluster table data by create_date, location_id, and device_version.
Cluster table data by create_date, partition by location_id, and device_version.

questions.explanation:
Partitioning by `create_date` lets BigQuery prune all partitions outside the most recent seven days. Clustering the remaining data by `location_id` and `device_version` lets BigQuery skip irrelevant storage blocks for those equality filters. BigQuery native tables support one partitioning column, while partitioning and clustering can be combined for finer-grained pruning.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to partitioned tables | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables) · [Querying clustered tables | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-clustered-tables)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are migrating a table to BigQuery and are choosing its data model. The table contains information about purchases made across multiple store locations, including the transaction time, purchased items, store ID, and the city and state where the store is located. You frequently query the table to determine how many of each item sold during the past 30 days and to analyze purchasing trends by state, city, and individual store. How should you model this table for optimal query performance?

options.text: Partition by transaction time; cluster by state first, then city, then store ID.
Partition by transaction time; cluster by store ID first, then city, then state.
Top-level cluster by state first, then city, then store ID.
Top-level cluster by store ID first, then city, then state.

questions.explanation:
Partitioning by transaction time allows BigQuery to prune partitions outside the 30-day reporting window. Clustering within each time partition by state, then city, then store ID aligns with the geographic filtering hierarchy. BigQuery gives precedence to earlier clustering columns and achieves the best block pruning when filters follow the clustering-column order.

**Learn more:** [Querying clustered tables | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-clustered-tables?hl=en) · [Introduction to partitioned tables | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is implementing a BigQuery data warehouse, and you have been assigned to design the data model. You migrate an on-premises sales data warehouse with a star schema to BigQuery, but observe performance issues when querying data from the last 30 days. Based on Google's recommended practices, what should you do to accelerate the query without increasing storage costs?

options.text: Denormalize the data.
Shard the data by customer ID.
Materialize the dimensional data in views.
Partition the data by transaction date.

questions.explanation:
Partitioning the fact data by transaction date allows BigQuery to prune partitions outside the requested 30-day range. It scans only the relevant date partitions, which improves query performance and reduces the bytes processed without adding duplicate stored data.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to partitioned tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables) · [Query partitioned tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-partitioned-tables)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing BigQuery tables for high volumes of clickstream event data. Your data analyst team will most often query specific event-date ranges and filter on the user ID UUID. You want to optimize the table structure for query cost and performance. What should you do?

options.text: Partition the table by the user ID column and cluster the table by the event date column.
Create an ingestion-time partitioned table and cluster it by the user ID column.
Cluster the table by both the event date and the user ID columns.
Partition the table by the event date column and cluster the table by user ID column.

questions.explanation:
Partitioning on the event date allows BigQuery to prune nonmatching date partitions, reducing bytes scanned for date-range queries. Clustering the data within each date partition by user ID lets BigQuery prune blocks for UUID filters, improving performance and reducing query cost.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to partitioned tables](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables) · [Create clustered tables](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/creating-clustered-tables)

The company uses distinct Google Cloud projects for development, staging, and production. Developers require edit access to the development project, read-only access to the staging project, and no access to the production project. You need an effective, manageable way to assign and enforce these permissions in line with Google-recommended practices. What should you do?

options.text: Create separate VPC Service Controls perimeters for each project and use access levels.
Grant individual developers specific IAM roles directly on each project.
Configure firewall rules within each project’s VPC to block traffic from unauthorized developer machines.
Create Google Groups for access levels, assign developers to groups, and grant the groups the appropriate IAM roles on each project.

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud recommends using access groups to model job functions and granting IAM roles to groups rather than to individual users. Group membership centrally manages the developers’ permissions: assign the appropriate edit role in development and read-only role in staging to the relevant groups, while granting no IAM role in production. IAM roles control resource access; network firewalls, VPC Service Controls, and access levels do not replace these project-level IAM grants.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],MJTelco is creating a custom interface for sharing data. It has these requirements:  
  
1. It must perform aggregations across its petabyte-scale datasets.  
2. It must scan rows in a specific time range with a very fast response time (milliseconds).

BigQuery and Cloud Bigtable
BigQuery and Cloud Storage

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Different teams in your organization store customer and performance data in BigQuery. Each team must retain full control of the data it collects, be able to query data in its own projects, and exchange data with other teams. You need to implement an organization-wide solution while minimizing operational effort and cost. What should you do?

Ask each team to publish their data in Analytics Hub. Direct the other teams to subscribe to them.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company generates reports from data stored in BigQuery. You want a quick, no-code solution. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Data Fusion and Wrangler to normalize the data, and set up a recurring job.
Use Dataflow SQL to create a job that normalizes the data, and that after the first run of the job, schedule the pipeline to execute recurrently.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have Node.js Cloud Functions that pull messages from Cloud Pub/Sub and write the data to BigQuery. You notice that the Pub/Sub topic’s message-processing rate is orders of magnitude higher than expected, with no error recorded in Cloud Logging. What are the two most likely causes of this issue? (Choose two.)

options.text: Publisher throughput quota is too small.
Total outstanding messages exceed the 10-MB maximum.
Error handling in the subscriber code is not handling run-time errors properly.
The subscriber code cannot keep up with the messages.
The subscriber code does not acknowledge the messages that it pulls.

questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub redelivers messages that are not acknowledged before the acknowledgment deadline. A subscriber that cannot keep pace can let acknowledgments expire, producing duplicate deliveries and potentially an escalating redelivery load. A subscriber that does not acknowledge pulled messages likewise causes repeated delivery of those messages.

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building an application on Google Cloud that automatically generates subject labels for users’ blog posts. You are testing a Dataflow pipeline that ingests and transforms text files. The files are gzip-compressed, errors are sent to a dead-letter queue, and you are using SideInputs to join data. You have noticed that the pipeline takes longer than expected to finish; what should you do to speed up the Dataflow job?

options.text: Switch to compressed Avro files.
Reduce the batch size.
Retry records that throw an error.
Use CoGroupByKey instead of the SideInput.

questions.explanation:
SideInputs materialize the entire join dataset to every worker, so once the joined data grows beyond the recommended size (~100 MB in streaming, under ~1 GB in batch) they become the bottleneck and slow the pipeline. Google's own Dataflow use-case guidance says to use SideInputs only for small lookup tables and to switch to a CoGroupByKey (a shuffle-based join) when both collections are larger, which distributes work evenly across workers. Switching to Avro (A) helps splittability of the source read but does not address the join cost that is described as the problem, reducing batch size (B) hurts throughput, and retrying errored records (C) adds work rather than removing it. Therefore replacing the SideInput join with CoGroupByKey is the correct optimization.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow use-case patterns (Part 2)](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/guide-to-common-cloud-dataflow-use-case-patterns-part-2)
