You are designing a data mesh on Google Cloud in which multiple distinct data engineering teams build data products. The typical data-curation pattern consists of:  
  
- Landing files in Cloud Storage  
- Transforming raw data in Cloud Storage and BigQuery datasets  
- Storing the final curated data product in BigQuery datasets  
  
You need to configure Dataplex so that each team can access only the assets required to build its data products. You must also ensure that teams can easily share the curated data product. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Create a single Dataplex virtual lake and create a single zone to contain landing, raw, and curated data.2. Provide each data engineering team access to the virtual lake.

1. Create a single Dataplex virtual lake and create a single zone to contain landing, raw, and curated data.2. Build separate assets for each data product within the zone.3. Assign permissions to the data engineering teams at the zone level.

1. Create a Dataplex virtual lake for each data product, and create a single zone to contain landing, raw, and curated data.2. Provide the data engineering teams with full access to the virtual lake assigned to their data product.

1. Create a Dataplex virtual lake for each data product, and create multiple zones for landing, raw, and curated data.2. Provide the data engineering teams with full access to the virtual lake assigned to their data product.

questions.explanation:
A separate Dataplex virtual lake for each data product isolates ownership and access to that product’s assets. Separate landing, raw, and curated zones represent the data lifecycle and expose the curated output as a distinct, shareable data-product boundary. Google Cloud guidance recommends raw and curated zones for each data-mesh domain and permits additional zones for granular team management and data contracts.

**Learn more:** [Build a data mesh](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataplex/docs/build-a-data-mesh-quickstart) · [Knowledge Catalog IAM permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataplex/docs/iam-permissions)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are working on a sensitive project that involves private user data. You have created a Google Cloud Platform project to hold this work internally. An external consultant will help code a complex transformation in a Google Cloud Dataflow pipeline for the project. How should you preserve users' privacy?

options.text: Grant the consultant the Viewer role on the project.
Grant the consultant the Cloud Dataflow Developer role on the project.
Create a service account and allow the consultant to log on with it.
Create an anonymized sample of the data for the consultant to work with in a different project.

questions.explanation:
An anonymized, de-identified sample in a separate project lets an external developer build and test the transformation without access to identifiable user data or the internal production project. Google Cloud documents Dataflow-based de-identification of sensitive data and recommends granting only the minimum permissions required, at the lowest practical resource level.

**Learn more:** [De-identification and re-identification of PII in large-scale datasets using Sensitive Data Protection](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/de-identification-re-identification-pii-using-cloud-dlp) · [Dataflow security and permissions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/security-and-permissions)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have a data pipeline that writes data to Cloud Bigtable with well-designed row keys. You want to monitor the pipeline to decide when to increase the size of your Cloud Bigtable cluster. Which two actions can you take to do this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Review Key Visualizer metrics. Increase the size of the Cloud Bigtable cluster when the Read pressure index is above 100.
Review Key Visualizer metrics. Increase the size of the Cloud Bigtable cluster when the Write pressure index is above 100.
Monitor the latency of write operations. Increase the size of the Cloud Bigtable cluster when there is a sustained increase in write latency.
Monitor storage utilization. Increase the size of the Cloud Bigtable cluster when utilization increases above 70% of max capacity.
Monitor latency of read operations. Increase the size of the Cloud Bigtable cluster of read operations take longer than 100 ms.

questions.explanation:
For evenly distributed Bigtable writes, a sustained increase in write latency can indicate that the cluster needs more capacity, and adding nodes spreads the workload across more nodes. Storage capacity also affects performance: for throughput optimization, Bigtable recommends maintaining storage utilization at no more than 70% of maximum capacity. Key Visualizer pressure indices identify problematic row keys or ranges and ordinarily call for schema or application changes rather than cluster scaling.

**Learn more:** [Understand performance | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/performance) · [Use Key Visualizer | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/keyvis-getting-started)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must assign new website users a globally unique identifier (GUID) by using a service that accepts data points and returns a GUID. The data comes from internal and external systems through HTTP calls made by microservices within your pipeline. There will be tens of thousands of messages per second, which can be multi-threaded, and you are concerned about system backpressure. How should you design the pipeline to minimize that backpressure?

options.text: Call out to the service via HTTP.
Create the pipeline statically in the class definition.
Create a new object in the startBundle method of DoFn.
Batch the job into ten-second increments.

questions.explanation:
For high-throughput writes or service calls, reuse a persistent client or network connection across a bundle rather than creating one for every element. Apache Beam specifically recommends initializing persistent connections in a DoFn’s `setup` or `startBundle` method; this reduces per-message connection overhead while bundles can be processed in parallel.

**Learn more:** [Apache Beam: Developing a new I/O connector](https://beam.apache.org/documentation/io/developing-io-overview/)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are running a streaming Cloud Dataflow pipeline. Your engineers have a new pipeline version that uses a different windowing algorithm and triggering strategy. You want to update the active pipeline to this new version while ensuring that no data is lost during the update. What should you do?

options.text: Update the Cloud Dataflow pipeline inflight by passing the --update option with the --jobName set to the existing job name
Update the Cloud Dataflow pipeline inflight by passing the --update option with the --jobName set to a new unique job name
Stop the Cloud Dataflow pipeline with the Cancel option. Create a new Cloud Dataflow job with the updated code
Stop the Cloud Dataflow pipeline with the Drain option. Create a new Cloud Dataflow job with the updated code

questions.explanation:
A Dataflow replacement update is launched with `--update` and the same job name as the running job. Dataflow performs a compatibility check and transfers compatible intermediate state and buffered or in-flight records to the replacement job. Windowing and trigger strategies can be changed in a replacement pipeline; those changes do not affect data already buffered or in flight.

**Learn more:** [Update an existing pipeline | Cloud Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/updating-a-pipeline)

questions.domain: Preparing and using data for analysis
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],After migrating ETL jobs to run on BigQuery, you need to confirm that the migrated jobs produce the same output as the original jobs. You have loaded a table containing the original job’s output and want to compare its contents with the output from the migrated job to demonstrate that they are identical. The tables have no primary-key column that would let you join them for comparison.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Select random samples from the tables using the RAND() function and compare the samples.
Select random samples from the tables using the HASH() function and compare the samples.
Use a Dataproc cluster and the BigQuery Hadoop connector to read the data from each table and calculate a hash from non-timestamp columns of the table after sorting. Compare the hashes of each table.
Create stratified random samples using the OVER() function and compare equivalent samples from each table.

questions.explanation:
A hash over every relevant row and non-timestamp column provides a full-data comparison rather than a probabilistic sample. Sorting before hashing removes differences caused by table row order, while excluding timestamp columns avoids false mismatches from execution-dependent timestamps. Dataproc can read BigQuery tables through the BigQuery Hadoop connector and calculate the hashes at scale.

**Learn more:** [Schema and data transfer overview — BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/migration/schema-data-overview) · [Overview: Migrate data warehouses to BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/migration/migration-overview)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are rolling out 10,000 new Internet of Things devices to gather temperature data in warehouses worldwide. You need to process, store, and analyze these very large datasets in real time. What should you do?

options.text: Send the data to Google Cloud Datastore and then export to BigQuery.
Send the data to Google Cloud Pub/Sub, stream Cloud Pub/Sub to Google Cloud Dataflow, and store the data in Google BigQuery.
Send the data to Cloud Storage and then spin up an Apache Hadoop cluster as needed in Google Cloud Dataproc whenever analysis is required.
Export logs in batch to Google Cloud Storage and then spin up a Google Cloud SQL instance, import the data from Cloud Storage, and run an analysis as needed.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Pub/Sub can ingest and distribute the continuous device-event stream at scale. Dataflow performs low-latency streaming processing and can transform or aggregate records before writing them to BigQuery, which serves as the analytics data warehouse. This Pub/Sub-to-Dataflow-to-BigQuery architecture supports real-time processing, storage, and analysis of high-volume sensor data.

**Learn more:** [Dataflow overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/overview) · [Stream from Pub/Sub to BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/tutorials/dataflow-stream-to-bigquery)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have critical legal-hold documents in a Cloud Storage bucket. You must ensure that these documents cannot be deleted or modified. What should you do?

options.text: Set a retention policy. Lock the retention policy.
Set a retention policy. Set the default storage class to Archive for long-term digital preservation.
Enable the Object Versioning feature. Add a lifecycle rule.
Enable the Object Versioning feature. Create a copy in a bucket in a different region.

questions.explanation:
A Cloud Storage bucket retention policy prevents objects from being deleted or replaced until their retention period has elapsed. Locking that policy permanently prevents it from being removed or shortened, providing immutable retention appropriate for legal-hold records.

**Learn more:** [Bucket Lock | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock) · [Use and lock retention policies | Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/using-bucket-lock?hl=en)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to analyze hundreds of thousands of social media posts each day at the lowest cost and with the fewest steps.  
  
You have the following requirements:  
  
- You will batch-load the posts once daily and process them with the Cloud Natural Language API.  
- You will extract topics and sentiment from the posts.  
- You must retain the raw posts for archiving and reprocessing.  
- You will create dashboards to share with people both inside and outside your organization.  
  
You need to store both the data extracted by the API for analysis and the raw social media posts for historical archival. What should you do?

options.text: Store the social media posts and the data extracted from the API in BigQuery.
Store the social media posts and the data extracted from the API in Cloud SQL.
Store the raw social media posts in Cloud Storage, and write the data extracted from the API into BigQuery.
Feed to social media posts into the API directly from the source, and write the extracted data from the API into BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Storage provides scalable object storage and low-cost archive storage for retaining raw posts, while BigQuery is a serverless analytics data warehouse optimized for large-scale analytical queries and business-intelligence dashboards. Storing raw source content in Cloud Storage and structured Natural Language API results in BigQuery supports inexpensive historical retention, reprocessing, and efficient analysis.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/introduction?hl=en) · [Storage classes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/storage-classes)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have created a new version of a Dataflow streaming data-ingestion pipeline that reads from Pub/Sub and writes to BigQuery. The prior version running in production uses a 5-minute processing window. You must deploy the new pipeline version without losing data, causing inconsistencies, or increasing processing latency by more than 10 minutes. What should you do?

options.text: Update the old pipeline with the new pipeline code.
Snapshot the old pipeline, stop the old pipeline, and then start the new pipeline from the snapshot.
Drain the old pipeline, then start the new pipeline.
Cancel the old pipeline, then start the new pipeline.

questions.explanation:
Dataflow snapshots save the state of a streaming pipeline and can include snapshots of its Pub/Sub sources. Starting the replacement job from that snapshot preserves processing state and source position, allowing the new version to resume without data loss or inconsistent windowed results. Draining instead closes in-progress windows and can emit partial or incomplete window results.

**Learn more:** [Use Dataflow snapshots](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/using-snapshots) · [Upgrade a streaming pipeline](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/upgrade-guide)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a new deep learning model to predict a customer’s likelihood of making a purchase on your ecommerce site. After evaluating the model using both the original training data and new test data, you determine that the model is overfitting. You want to increase the model’s accuracy when it predicts new data. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the size of the training dataset, and increase the number of input features.
Increase the size of the training dataset, and decrease the number of input features.
Reduce the size of the training dataset, and increase the number of input features.
Reduce the size of the training dataset, and decrease the number of input features.

questions.explanation:
Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes training patterns rather than generalizing to unseen data. More training examples can improve generalization, and reducing the number of input features lowers model flexibility and decreases the risk of learning spurious patterns.

**Learn more:** [Model Fit: Underfitting vs. Overfitting - Amazon Machine Learning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/latest/dg/model-fit-underfitting-vs-overfitting.html) · [Training Parameters - Amazon Machine Learning](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/machine-learning/latest/dg/training-parameters.html)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are part of the data governance team and are implementing security requirements for resource deployment. You must ensure that resources are restricted to only the `europe-west3` region and want to follow Google-recommended practices.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Set the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations organization policy constraint to in:europe-west3-locations.
Deploy resources with Terraform and implement a variable validation rule to ensure that the region is set to the europe-west3 region for all resources.
Set the constraints/gcp.resourceLocations organization policy constraint to in:eu-locations.
Create a Cloud Function to monitor all resources created and automatically destroy the ones created outside the europe-west3 region.

questions.explanation:
The `constraints/gcp.resourceLocations` Organization Policy constraint centrally prevents creation of supported resources outside the allowed locations. Google recommends value groups for location policies; `in:europe-west3-locations` represents the `europe-west3` region and its zones, enforcing the required regional boundary. [Restrict resource locations](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/restrict-locations)

**Learn more:** [Google Cloud: Restrict resource locations](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/restrict-locations) · [Google Cloud: Organization policy constraints](https://cloud.google.com/organization-policy/reference/org-policy-constraints)

You enabled the free Firebase Analytics–Google BigQuery integration. Firebase now automatically creates a new BigQuery table each day, using the format `app_events_YYYYMMDD`.  
  
You want to query every table from the last 30 days using legacy SQL. What should you do?

options.text: Use the TABLE_DATE_RANGE function
Use the WHERE_PARTITIONTIME pseudo column
Use WHERE date BETWEEN YYYY-MM-DD AND YYYY-MM-DD
Use SELECT IF.(date >= YYYY-MM-DD AND date <= YYYY-MM-DD

questions.explanation:
`TABLE_DATE_RANGE` is the legacy BigQuery SQL wildcard function for querying multiple daily tables whose names follow the `<prefix>YYYYMMDD` pattern. It can select the `app_events_` tables that fall within a 30-day timestamp range.\
\
**Learn more:** [Legacy SQL syntax, functions, and operators](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/legacy-sql)

questions.question:
You enabled the free Firebase Analytics–Google BigQuery integration. Firebase now automatically creates a new BigQuery table each day, using the format `app_events_YYYYMMDD`.  
  
You want to query every table from the last 30 days using legacy SQL. What should you do?

options.text: Create a view with a filter to drop rows with fewer than 8 vCPU, and use the UNNEST operator.
Create a materialized view with a filter to drop rows with fewer than 8 vCPU, and use the WITH common table expression.
Create a view with a filter to drop rows with fewer than 8 vCPU, and use the WITH common table expression.
Use Dataflow to batch process and write the result to another BigQuery table.

questions.explanation:
The VM components are stored as repeated records, so `UNNEST` is needed to expose each component record and filter the `vcpu` component by its quantity. A logical view centralizes that filtering query for reporting without requiring a separate Dataflow batch pipeline or a duplicate output table.

**Learn more:** [Work with arrays | BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/arrays) · [UNNEST operator | BigQuery query syntax](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/query-syntax)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have **15 TB** of data in your on-premises data center that you need to transfer to Google Cloud. The data changes weekly and resides on a POSIX-compliant source. The network operations team has allocated **500 Mbps** of public-internet bandwidth.  
  
You want to follow Google-recommended practices to transfer the data reliably to Google Cloud each week. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger the gsutil command. Use the -m parameter for optimal parallelism.
Use Transfer Appliance to migrate your data into a Google Kubernetes Engine cluster, and then configure a weekly transfer job.
Install Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data in your data center, and then configure a weekly transfer job.
Install Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data on a Google Cloud virtual machine, and then configure a weekly transfer job.

questions.explanation:
Storage Transfer Service supports agent-based transfers from on-premises POSIX file systems to Cloud Storage. Installing its agents on infrastructure in the data center that can access the source enables managed, incremental transfer jobs on a weekly schedule, with retries and monitoring. Storage Transfer Service is designed for large-scale data transfers and recurring synchronization. [Transfer from a file system to Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/create-transfers/agent-based/file-system-to-cloud-storage), [Schedule transfers](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/schedule-transfer-jobs)

**Learn more:** [Transfer from a file system to Cloud Storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/create-transfers/agent-based/file-system-to-cloud-storage) · [Schedule transfers](https://cloud.google.com/storage-transfer/docs/schedule-transfer-jobs)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are moving an application that tracks library books and information about every book, such as its author or publication year, from an on-premises data warehouse to BigQuery. In the existing relational database, author information is stored in a separate table and joined to book information by a common key. Based on Google's recommended schema-design practice, how should you organize the data to provide optimal query speed for author information for each borrowed book?

options.text: Keep the schema the same, maintain the different tables for the book and each of the attributes, and query as you are doing today.
Create a table that is wide and includes a column for each attribute, including the author's first name, last name, date of birth, etc.
Create a table that includes information about the books and authors, but nest the author fields inside the author column.
Keep the schema the same, create a view that joins all of the tables, and always query the view.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery recommends denormalizing frequently queried hierarchical relationships with nested and repeated fields. Storing author attributes as nested fields in the book record preserves the relationship while avoiding the data coordination and performance cost of repeatedly joining separate book and author tables.

**Learn more:** [Specify nested and repeated columns in table schemas](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/nested-repeated) · [Use nested and repeated fields](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/best-practices-performance-nested)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are preparing data to serve a sales-demand prediction model. The training data goes through several preprocessing steps, including scaling numerical features and one-hot encoding categorical features. The model is deployed on Vertex AI Endpoints. You need to avoid training-serving skew and ensure accurate production predictions. You want an easy-to-implement solution.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Implement a custom handler within the Vertex AI Endpoint to automatically perform data transformations before the model makes a prediction.
Replicate the exact same pre-processing logic in the inference pipeline that was used during model training.
Store the raw, unprocessed data in a separate Cloud Storage bucket exclusively for serving.
Ensure the serving data is a smaller, random sample of the training data.

questions.explanation:
Training-serving skew is avoided by supplying model inputs in exactly the same form at serving time as during training. Applying the identical numerical-scaling and categorical one-hot-encoding logic in the inference pipeline preserves the expected feature values, order, and representation for reliable predictions.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to tabular data | Vertex AI | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/tabular-data/tabular101)

Your company needs to retrieve large medical-information result sets from its current system, whose database contains more than 10 TB, and save the data in new tables for subsequent queries. The database must use a low-maintenance architecture and be available through SQL. You need to implement a cost-effective solution that supports analytics on large result sets. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud SQL, but first organize the data into tables. Use JOIN in queries to retrieve data.
Use BigQuery as a data warehouse. Set output destinations for caching large queries.
Use a MySQL cluster installed on a Compute Engine managed instance group for scalability.
Use Cloud Spanner to replicate the data across regions. Normalize the data in a series of tables.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery is a fully managed analytics data warehouse that supports GoogleSQL and large-scale analytical queries. Query results can be written to a destination table, including a newly created table, so large result sets can be retained and queried later without operating database infrastructure. [Writing query results](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/writing-results)

**Learn more:** [Writing query results | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/writing-results) · [Introduction to SQL in BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/introduction-sql)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You create a data source that retains the most recent 6 weeks of data and build visualizations that let viewers select multiple date ranges, distinct geographic regions, and unique installation types. The newest data must always be displayed without changing the visualizations, and you want to avoid creating and updating visualizations every month. What should you do?

![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783787460671-6ez9o5qi.png)

![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783787464169-yu9d4ocm.png)

options.text: Look through the current data and compose a series of charts and tables, one for each possible combination of criteria.
Look through the current data and compose a small set of generalized charts and tables bound to criteria filters that allow value selection.
Export the data to a spreadsheet, compose a series of charts and tables, one for each possible combination of criteria, and spread them across multiple tabs.

Load the data into relational database tables, write a Google App Engine application that queries all rows, summarizes the data across each criteria, and then renders results using the Google Charts and visualization API.

questions.explanation:
Generalized charts and tables can be bound to date-range and dimension filter controls, allowing viewers to select values such as geography and installation type while the visualizations continue to query the current data source. This keeps a single reusable report current as new data arrives, without maintaining separate visualizations for each combination or month.

**Learn more:** [About controls | Data Studio | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/data-studio/about-controls) · [Bar chart and column chart reference | Looker Studio | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/bar-chart-and-column-chart-reference)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a bank. You have a labelled dataset containing information about previously granted loan applications and whether those applications defaulted. You have been asked to train a model to predict default rates for credit applicants.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Increase the size of the dataset by collecting additional data.
Train a linear regression to predict a credit default risk score.
Remove the bias from the data and collect applications that have been declined loans.
Match loan applicants with their social profiles to enable feature engineering.

questions.explanation: Loan-default labels from only approved applications introduce selection bias because approved borrowers are not necessarily representative of the full credit-applicant population. Addressing that bias requires including declined applications in the data-collection process so the training data better represents the population for which default predictions are needed.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team develops and maintains the company's ETL pipelines. A Dataflow job is failing because its input data contains errors, and you need to improve the pipeline's reliability, including the ability to reprocess all failed data.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Add a filtering step to skip these types of errors in the future, extract erroneous rows from logs.
Add a tryג€¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, extract erroneous rows from logs.
Add a tryג€¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, write erroneous rows to Pub/Sub PubSub directly from the DoFn.
Add a tryג€¦ catch block to your DoFn that transforms the data, use a sideOutput to create a PCollection that can be stored to Pub/Sub later.

questions.explanation:
A dead-letter-queue pattern catches per-record exceptions in the transformation and routes failed elements through a branching (side) output into a separate `PCollection`. That collection can be written to Pub/Sub as a normal pipeline sink and retained for inspection and reprocessing. This avoids losing records in logs and avoids non-idempotent external publishing directly within a retried `DoFn`. [Dataflow pipeline best practices](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/pipeline-best-practices)

**Learn more:** [Dataflow pipeline best practices](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/pipeline-best-practices) · [Read from Pub/Sub to Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-with-cloud-pubsub)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You must load a multi-terabyte clickstream dataset into BigQuery. The data arrives daily as compressed JSON files in a Cloud Storage bucket. You require a low-cost, programmatic, scalable way to load the data into BigQuery. What should you do?

options.text: Create an external table in BigQuery pointing to the Cloud Storage bucket and run the INSERT INTO ... SELECT * FROM external_table command.
Use the BigQuery Data Transfer Service from Cloud Storage.
Create a Cloud Run function to run a Python script to read and parse each JSON file, and use the BigQuery streaming insert API.
Use Cloud Data Fusion to create a pipeline to load the JSON files into BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery Data Transfer Service provides a managed Cloud Storage connector for scheduled, recurring loads into BigQuery. It supports newline-delimited JSON and supported compressed inputs, uses scalable BigQuery load jobs, and can be configured programmatically, avoiding custom streaming-insert code or an ETL pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Load Cloud Storage data into BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/cloud-storage-transfer) · [Introduction to Cloud Storage transfers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/cloud-storage-transfer-overview)

questions.domain: Preparing and using data for analysis
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses Looker Studio connected to BigQuery for reporting. Users experience slow dashboard load times because complex queries run against a large table. The queries include aggregations and filtering across several columns. You need to optimize query performance to reduce dashboard load times. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Looker Studio to use a shorter data refresh interval to ensure fresh data is always displayed.
Create a materialized view in BigQuery that pre-calculates the aggregations and filters used in the Looker Studio dashboards.
Implement row-level security in BigQuery to restrict data access and reduce the amount of data processed by the queries.
Use BigQuery BI Engine to accelerate query performance by caching frequently accessed data.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery materialized views precompute and store query results, including eligible aggregations and filters, and can be incrementally maintained as base-table data changes. Directing repeated dashboard workloads to this pre-aggregated data avoids repeatedly executing expensive operations against the large source table, reducing query latency.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to materialized views | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/materialized-views-intro)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use BigQuery with a multi-region dataset that contains a table of daily sales volumes. The table is updated several times each day. You must protect the sales table against regional failures with an RPO of less than 24 hours while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Schedule a daily export of the table to a Cloud Storage dual or multi-region bucket.
Schedule a daily copy of the dataset to a backup region.
Schedule a daily BigQuery snapshot of the table.
Modify ETL job to load the data into both the current and another backup region.

questions.explanation:
A dual- or multi-region Cloud Storage export provides a separate, geographically resilient backup at lower storage cost than maintaining a second BigQuery dataset or dual-loading every update. BigQuery table snapshots are constrained to the source table’s region, and selecting a BigQuery multi-region location does not itself provide cross-region replication or regional-outage redundancy.

**Learn more:** [Cross-region dataset replication | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/data-replication) · [Backup & Disaster Recovery strategies for BigQuery | Google Cloud Blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/backup-disaster-recovery-strategies-bigquery)

Your organization has collected and analyzed data in Google BigQuery for 6 months. Most of the data analyzed is stored in a time-partitioned table named `events_partitioned`. To lower query costs, the organization created a view named `events` that queries only the most recent 14 days of data. The view is defined in legacy SQL.  
  
Next month, existing applications will connect to BigQuery through an ODBC connection to read the `events` data. You need to ensure that the applications can connect. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create a new view over events using standard SQL
Create a new partitioned table using a standard SQL query
Create a new view over events_partitioned using standard SQL
Create a service account for the ODBC connection to use for authentication
Create a Google Cloud Identity and Access Management (Cloud IAM) role for the ODBC connection and shared ג€eventsג€

questions.explanation:
A GoogleSQL query cannot reference a view defined with legacy SQL. A new GoogleSQL view must therefore query `events_partitioned` directly while applying the existing 14-day restriction. BigQuery’s ODBC driver supports service-account authentication, so a service account can supply the credentials used by the applications.

**Learn more:** [Create logical views — BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/views) · [Use the ODBC driver for BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/odbc-for-bigquery)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have three years of historical data in BigQuery, and a data pipeline delivers new data to BigQuery each day. You noticed that when the Data Science team runs a query filtered on a date column and restricted to 30–90 days of data, it scans the entire table. You also observed that your bill is rising faster than expected. You want to fix the issue as cost-effectively as possible while retaining the ability to run SQL queries.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Re-create the tables using DDL. Partition the tables by a column containing a TIMESTAMP or DATE Type.
Recommend that the Data Science team export the table to a CSV file on Cloud Storage and use Cloud Datalab to explore the data by reading the files directly.
Modify your pipeline to maintain the last 30ג€
Write an Apache Beam pipeline that creates a BigQuery table per day. Recommend that the Data Science team use wildcards on the table name suffixes to select the data they need.

questions.explanation:
A table partitioned on the relevant `DATE` or `TIMESTAMP` column allows BigQuery to prune partitions when a query filters that column. Queries for a 30–90-day range therefore scan only the matching partitions rather than the entire three-year table, lowering bytes processed and query cost while preserving SQL access.

**Learn more:** [Query partitioned tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-partitioned-tables?hl=en) · [Introduction to partitioned tables | BigQuery | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables?hl=en)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses WILDCARD tables to query data across several similarly named tables. The SQL statement is currently failing with this error:  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783810383033-x8nywoit.png)  
  
Which table name makes the SQL statement work correctly?

options.text: 'bigquery-public-data.noaa_gsod.gsod'
bigquery-public-data.noaa_gsod.gsod*
'bigquery-public-data.noaa_gsod.gsod'*
'bigquery-public-data.noaa_gsod.gsod*`

questions.explanation:
A BigQuery wildcard table name must place `*` at the end of the table prefix and enclose the entire table identifier in backticks. Backticks allow the hyphens in `bigquery-public-data` and the wildcard character to be parsed correctly; single quotation marks denote string literals rather than table identifiers. [Query multiple tables using a wildcard table](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-wildcard-tables?hl=en)

**Learn more:** [Query multiple tables using a wildcard table](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/querying-wildcard-tables?hl=en)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You operate a Cloud Dataflow streaming pipeline. The pipeline aggregates events from a Cloud Pub/Sub subscription source within a window and writes the resulting aggregation to a Cloud Storage bucket. The source has consistent throughput. You want to monitor the pipeline’s behavior with a Cloud Stackdriver alert to ensure that it is processing data. Which Stackdriver alerts should you create?

options.text: An alert based on a decrease of subscription/num_undelivered_messages for the source and a rate of change increase of instance/storage/ used_bytes for the destination
An alert based on an increase of subscription/num_undelivered_messages for the source and a rate of change decrease of instance/storage/ used_bytes for the destination
An alert based on a decrease of instance/storage/used_bytes for the source and a rate of change increase of subscription/ num_undelivered_messages for the destination
An alert based on an increase of instance/storage/used_bytes for the source and a rate of change decrease of subscription/ num_undelivered_messages for the destination

questions.explanation:
A growing Pub/Sub subscription backlog means subscribers are not keeping pace with incoming messages. A pipeline that continues to process and write results should cause the destination bucket’s used storage to grow; a decrease in that growth rate indicates reduced or stopped output. These conditions together detect a stalled or underperforming pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Monitor Pub/Sub in Cloud Monitoring](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/monitoring) · [Google Cloud metrics: P through Z](https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/api/metrics_gcp_p_z)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a large ecommerce company and use Pub/Sub to ingest clickstream data into Google Cloud for analytics. You observe that when a new subscriber connects to an existing topic to analyze data, it cannot subscribe to older data. For an upcoming yearly sale event in two months, you need a solution that, once implemented, enables any new subscriber to read the last 30 days of data. What should you do?

options.text: Create a new topic, and publish the last 30 days of data each time a new subscriber connects to an existing topic.
Set the topic retention policy to 30 days.
Set the subscriber retention policy to 30 days.
Ask the source system to re-push the data to Pub/Sub, and subscribe to it.

questions.explanation:
Pub/Sub topic message retention retains messages after publication for the configured period, independently of individual subscriptions. Retaining messages on the topic for 30 days allows a new subscription to replay the retained historical messages, whereas subscription retention applies only after that individual subscription is created.

**Learn more:** [Topic properties | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/topic-properties) · [Replay and purge messages with seek | Pub/Sub | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/replay-overview)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is currently establishing data pipelines for its campaign. For all Google Cloud Pub/Sub streaming data, an important business requirement is to periodically identify the inputs and their timings throughout the campaign.  
  
Engineers have decided to use windowing and transformation in Google Cloud Dataflow for this purpose. However, while testing this feature, they find that the Cloud Dataflow job fails for all streaming inserts. What is the most likely cause of this issue?

options.text: They have not assigned the timestamp, which causes the job to fail
They have not set the triggers to accommodate the data coming in late, which causes the job to fail
They have not applied a global windowing function, which causes the job to fail when the pipeline is created
They have not applied a non-global windowing function, which causes the job to fail when the pipeline is created

questions.explanation:
Google Cloud Pub/Sub data is unbounded. In Dataflow, applying grouping or aggregation to an unbounded PCollection in the default global window without a trigger is invalid at pipeline construction time. Using a finite, non-global window bounds the data for each periodic aggregation.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot and debug Dataflow pipelines](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/guides/troubleshooting-your-pipeline) · [Streaming pipelines](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-pipelines)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have data pipelines operating on BigQuery, Dataflow, and Dataproc. You need to perform health checks and monitor their behavior, then notify the team that manages the pipelines when they fail. You must also be able to work across multiple projects. You prefer to use managed platform products or features. What should you do?

options.text: Export the information to Cloud Monitoring, and set up an Alerting policy
Run a Virtual Machine in Compute Engine with Airflow, and export the information to Cloud Monitoring
Export the logs to BigQuery, and set up App Engine to read that information and send emails if you find a failure in the logs
Develop an App Engine application to consume logs using GCP API calls, and send emails if you find a failure in the logs

questions.explanation:
Cloud Monitoring provides managed monitoring and alerting for Google Cloud service metrics. Alerting policies evaluate defined conditions and use notification channels to notify the responsible team. A multi-project metrics scope lets one scoping project chart and monitor time-series data from multiple projects.

**Learn more:** [Configure a metrics scope](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings/multiple-projects) · [Alerting overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You maintain ETL pipelines. You observe that a streaming pipeline running on Dataflow takes a long time to process incoming data, causing delayed output. You also observe that Dataflow automatically optimized the pipeline graph and fused it into a single step. You want to determine where the potential bottleneck is occurring. What should you do?

options.text: Insert a Reshuffle operation after each processing step, and monitor the execution details in the Dataflow console.
Insert output sinks after each key processing step, and observe the writing throughput of each block.
Log debug information in each ParDo function, and analyze the logs at execution time.
Verify that the Dataflow service accounts have appropriate permissions to write the processed data to the output sinks.

questions.explanation:
Dataflow can fuse multiple transforms into one execution stage, which obscures where processing time is being spent. A Reshuffle creates a boundary that prevents the surrounding transforms from being fused, allowing the Dataflow console’s Execution details to show separate stages and identify the slow or bottlenecked stage.

**Learn more:** [Pipeline lifecycle — Cloud Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/pipeline-lifecycle) · [Execution details — Cloud Dataflow](https://cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/execution-details)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use BigQuery with a regional dataset that contains a table of daily sales volumes. The table is updated several times each day. You must protect the sales table from regional failures with a recovery point objective (RPO) of less than 24 hours while minimizing costs. What should you do?

options.text: Schedule a daily export of the table to a Cloud Storage dual or multi-region bucket.
Schedule a daily copy of the dataset to a backup region.
Schedule a daily BigQuery snapshot of the table.
Modify ETL job to load the data into both the current and another backup region.

questions.explanation:
A scheduled export to a dual- or multi-region Cloud Storage bucket places the backup outside the single BigQuery regional failure domain while using comparatively low-cost object storage. BigQuery table snapshots do not provide cross-region protection, whereas maintaining a second BigQuery dataset or writing every load to two regions costs more. Cloud Storage export frequency should be set according to the required RPO.

**Learn more:** [Understand reliability — BigQuery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reliability-intro?hl=en) · [Backup & Disaster Recovery strategies for BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/backup-disaster-recovery-strategies-bigquery/)

questions.question: Your neural-network model takes days to train. You want to speed up training. What can you do?

options.text: Subsample your test dataset.
Subsample your training dataset.
Increase the number of input features to your model.
Increase the number of layers in your neural network.

questions.explanation:
Subsampling the training dataset reduces the number of examples processed in each epoch, decreasing total training computation and time. A test dataset is used for evaluation rather than parameter updates, while more input features or additional neural-network layers generally increase training cost.\
\
**Learn more:** [Datasets: Transforming data](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/overfitting/transforming-data)

questions.question: Your neural-network model takes days to train. You want to speed up training. What can you do?

options.text: Provide latitude and longitude as input vectors to your neural net.
Create a numeric column from a feature cross of latitude and longitude.
Create a feature cross of latitude and longitude, bucketize it at the minute level and use L1 regularization during optimization.
Create a feature cross of latitude and longitude, bucketize it at the minute level and use L2 regularization during optimization.

questions.explanation:
Bucketed latitude and longitude should be crossed so the model can learn effects for geographic areas defined by their joint coordinates; a location is not captured adequately by either coordinate alone or by a cross of raw numeric values. The resulting fine-grained crossed feature is sparse, and L1 regularization promotes sparsity by driving uninformative feature weights to exactly zero.

**Learn more:** [Categorical data: Feature crosses](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/categorical-data/feature-crosses) · [Feature crosses knowledge check](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/MCE/mc-il-feature-crosses)

questions.domain: Preparing and using data for analysis
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You work for a manufacturing company that sources up to 750 different components, each from a separate supplier. You have collected a labeled dataset with an average of 1000 examples for every unique component. Your team wants to build an app that helps warehouse workers identify incoming components from a photo of the component. You want to deliver the first working version of this app as a Proof-Of-Concept within a few working days. What should you do?

options.text: Use Cloud Vision AutoML with the existing dataset.
Use Cloud Vision AutoML, but reduce your dataset twice.
Use Cloud Vision API by providing custom labels as recognition hints.
Train your own image recognition model leveraging transfer learning techniques.

questions.explanation:
Cloud Vision AutoML is designed to train a custom image-classification model from labeled images, making it appropriate for recognizing hundreds of organization-specific component categories with minimal model-development effort. The Cloud Vision API’s built-in label detection is intended for broad, predefined categories; it does not learn custom component labels from the dataset. Google Cloud documentation directs targeted custom-label use cases to AutoML Vision.

**Learn more:** [Detect Labels | Cloud Vision API | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vision/docs/labels?authuser=2)

options.text: Set the BigQuery dataset to be regional. In the event of an emergency, use a point-in-time snapshot to recover the data.

Set the BigQuery dataset to be regional. Create a scheduled query to make copies of the data to tables suffixed with the time of the backup. In the event of an emergency, use the backup copy of the table.
Set the BigQuery dataset to be multi-regional. In the event of an emergency, use a point-in-time snapshot to recover the data.

Set the BigQuery dataset to be multi-regional. Create a scheduled query to make copies of the data to tables suffixed with the time of the backup. In the event of an emergency, use the backup copy of the table.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery time travel supports recovery only within a window of up to seven days, so it cannot provide a 30-day recovery point. Scheduled timestamped table copies retain a recoverable backup for the required period. BigQuery stores a regional dataset redundantly across two zones, and choosing a multi-region location does not add cross-region redundancy or improve availability during a regional outage.

**Learn more:** [Data retention with time travel and fail-safe](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/time-travel) · [Cross-region dataset replication](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/data-replication)

You work for a farming company. You have a single BigQuery table named `sensors`, about 500 MB in size, that contains the list of your 5000 sensors with columns for `id`, `name`, and `location`. This table is updated hourly. Each sensor produces one metric every 30 seconds together with a timestamp, and you want to store those metrics in BigQuery. You want to run an analytical query on the data once per week for monitoring purposes. You also want to minimize costs. Which data model should you use?

options.text: 1. Create a metrics column in the sensors table.2. Set RECORD type and REPEATED mode for the metrics column.3. Use an UPDATE statement every 30 seconds to add new metrics.
1. Create a metrics column in the sensors table.2. Set RECORD type and REPEATED mode for the metrics column.3. Use an INSERT statement every 30 seconds to add new metrics.

1. Create a metrics table partitioned by timestamp.2. Create a sensorId column in the metrics table, that points to the id column in the sensors table.3. Use an INSERT statement every 30 seconds to append new metrics to the metrics table.4. Join the two tables, if needed, when running the analytical query.

1. Create a metrics table partitioned by timestamp.2. Create a sensorId column in the metrics table, which points to the id column in the sensors table.3. Use an UPDATE statement every 30 seconds to append new metrics to the metrics table.4. Join the two tables, if needed, when running the analytical query.

questions.explanation:
Store the high-volume, append-only time-series readings in a separate metrics table partitioned by timestamp, with `sensorId` relating each metric to the sensor metadata. Append new readings with `INSERT` and join to `sensors` only when metadata is needed. Timestamp partitioning limits data scanned by time-bounded analytics, and `INSERT` is less costly than `UPDATE` for adding new rows because BigQuery charges `UPDATE` for both the statement and the affected target-table data.

**Learn more:** [Data manipulation language (DML) statements in GoogleSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/dml-syntax) · [Updating partitioned table data using DML](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/using-dml-with-partitioned-tables)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a fraud-detection model with BigQuery ML. You have a raw transaction dataset and must create new features such as `average_transaction_amount_last_24_hours` and `time_since_last_transaction`. These features require aggregation and time-window calculations on the existing data. The objective is to ensure these features are applied consistently during both model training and prediction, without manual intervention. You need to prepare these features efficiently for the model. What should you do?

options.text: Implement a Cloud Run function that triggers on new transactions, calculates the features, and inserts them into a feature store before model serving.
Export the BigQuery data to Cloud Storage, perform feature engineering using a custom Python script in a Dataflow job, and then re-import the engineered features into BigQuery.
Use the TRANSFORM clause within the CREATE MODEL statement, leveraging SQL functions for aggregations and time-based calculations.
Create a separate BigQuery table containing pre-computed features using complex SQL queries and join this table with the raw data during model training and serving.

questions.explanation:
The requirement is that the feature engineering be applied identically at training and prediction time with no manual intervention. The TRANSFORM clause of CREATE MODEL stores the preprocessing logic inside the model, and ML.PREDICT and ML.EVALUATE automatically retrieve and reapply those exact transformations, eliminating training/serving skew. A feature store fed by a Cloud Run function (A), a Dataflow export/re-import (B), or a separate pre-computed feature table joined at serving time (D) all require you to reproduce and keep the logic in sync manually, which is precisely what the question wants to avoid. Using TRANSFORM inside the CREATE MODEL statement is therefore the efficient, consistent choice.

**Learn more:** [The TRANSFORM clause in BigQuery ML](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/bigqueryml-transform)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your startup has never established a formal security policy. At present, everyone in the company can access the datasets stored in Google BigQuery. Teams are free to use the service as they choose, and they have not documented their use cases. You have been asked to secure the data warehouse. You need to find out what everyone is doing. What should you do first?

options.text: Use Google Stackdriver Audit Logs to review data access.
Get the identity and access management IIAM) policy of each table
Use Stackdriver Monitoring to see the usage of BigQuery query slots.
Use the Google Cloud Billing API to see what account the warehouse is being billed to.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery Data Access audit logs record operational access to warehouse data, including table reads and table data changes, enabling discovery of actual users and usage patterns before access controls are redesigned. IAM policies show granted permissions, not necessarily how the data is being used.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery audit logs overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/auditlogs) · [Cloud Audit Logs overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You migrated an application's data backend that serves **10 PB** of historical product data for analytics. Only the latest known state of each product—approximately **10 GB** of data—must be exposed through an API to other applications.  
  
Choose a cost-effective persistent storage solution that supports the analytics requirements and API performance of up to **1000 queries per second (QPS)** with latency under **1 second**. What should you do?

options.text: 1. Store the historical data in BigQuery for analytics.2. Use a materialized view to precompute the last state of a product.3. Serve the last state data directly from BigQuery to the API.

1. Store the products as a collection in Firestore with each product having a set of historical changes.2. Use simple and compound queries for analytics.3. Serve the last state data directly from Firestore to the API.

1. Store the historical data in Cloud SQL for analytics.2. In a separate table, store the last state of the product after every product change.3. Serve the last state data directly from Cloud SQL to the API.

1. Store the historical data in BigQuery for analytics.2. In a Cloud SQL table, store the last state of the product after every product change.3. Serve the last state data directly from Cloud SQL to the API.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery is designed for large-scale analytical queries, including workloads spanning petabytes, so it is appropriate for the 10 PB historical dataset. Keeping the approximately 10 GB latest product state in Cloud SQL separates the high-rate operational API reads from the analytical workload; Cloud SQL can serve this smaller, indexed current-state table with low latency. This architecture avoids using an analytics warehouse as the API’s high-volume operational datastore.

**Learn more:** [BigQuery overview](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/introduction) · [Overview of BigQuery storage](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/storage_overview)

Join the two tables, if needed, when running the analytical query."},"correctAnswer":"C","explanation":"Store the high-volume, append-only time-series readings in a separate metrics table partitioned by timestamp, with `sensorId` relating each metric to the sensor metadata. You work for a large fast-food restaurant chain with more than 400,000 employees. Employee information is stored in Google BigQuery in a `Users` table containing `FirstName` and `LastName` fields. An IT team member is building an application and asks you to modify the BigQuery schema and data so the application can query a `FullName` field consisting, for every employee, of the `FirstName` value concatenated with a space and then the `LastName` value. How can you make this data available while minimizing cost?

options.text: Create a view in BigQuery that concatenates the FirstName and LastName field values to produce the FullName.
Add a new column called FullName to the Users table. Run an UPDATE statement that updates the FullName column for each user with the concatenation of the FirstName and LastName values.

Create a Google Cloud Dataflow job that queries BigQuery for the entire Users table, concatenates the FirstName value and LastName value for each user, and loads the proper values for FirstName, LastName, and FullName into a new table in BigQuery.

Use BigQuery to export the data for the table to a CSV file. Create a Google Cloud Dataproc job to process the CSV file and output a new CSV file containing the proper values for FirstName, LastName and FullName. Run a BigQuery load job to load the new CSV file into BigQuery.

questions.explanation:
A BigQuery logical view is a virtual table that can define `FullName` with a concatenation expression over `FirstName` and `LastName`, making the derived field queryable without storing duplicate data or updating all rows. Logical views have no physical data storage overhead; by contrast, an `UPDATE` of a non-partitioned table is billed for both the bytes scanned and the pre-update table size.

**Learn more:** [Introduction to logical views](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/views-intro) · [Data manipulation language (DML) statements in GoogleSQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/dml-syntax)

Industry government regulations require maintaining an auditable record of access to certain data types. Assuming that all logs that expire are archived correctly, where should data subject to this requirement be stored?

options.text: Encrypted on Cloud Storage with user-supplied encryption keys. A separate decryption key will be given to each authorized user.
In a BigQuery dataset that is viewable only by authorized personnel, with the Data Access log used to provide the auditability.
In Cloud SQL, with separate database user names to each user. The Cloud SQL Admin activity logs will be used to provide the auditability.
In a bucket on Cloud Storage that is accessible only by an AppEngine service that collects user information and logs the access before providing a link to the bucket.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery Data Access audit logs record API activity that reads, creates, modifies, or otherwise accesses user-provided data, providing an access audit trail. BigQuery is the exception for which Data Access audit logs are enabled by default. Admin Activity logs, such as those used for Cloud SQL administration, record changes to resource configuration or metadata rather than access to the stored data.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Audit Logs overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a streaming Dataflow pipeline that ingests noise-level data from hundreds of sensors located near construction sites throughout a city. The sensors measure noise levels every ten seconds and send data to the pipeline whenever levels exceed 70 dBA. You need to detect a sensor’s average noise level when data has been received for longer than 30 minutes, with the window ending after no data has been received for 15 minutes. What should you do?

options.text: Use session windows with a 15-minute gap duration.
Use session windows with a 30-minute gap duration.
Use hopping windows with a 15-minute window, and a thirty-minute period.
Use tumbling windows with a 15-minute window and a fifteen-minute .withAllowedLateness operator.

questions.explanation:
Session windows group events for the same key while successive events remain within the configured inactivity gap, and a later event begins a new session. A 15-minute session gap therefore closes a sensor’s activity window after 15 minutes without received data; the 30-minute threshold can be evaluated on that session’s duration before using its average.

**Learn more:** [Streaming pipelines | Cloud Dataflow | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/dataflow/docs/concepts/streaming-pipelines)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company generates 20,000 files per hour. Each data file is a comma-separated values (CSV) file smaller than 4 KB. Every file must be ingested into Google Cloud Platform before processing.  
  
Your company site has 200 ms latency to Google Cloud, and its Internet connection is limited to 50 Mbps. You currently use a secure FTP (SFTP) server on a Google Compute Engine virtual machine as the ingestion point. A local SFTP client running on a dedicated machine sends the CSV files unchanged. The objective is to make reports containing the previous day's data available to executives by 10:00 a.m. daily. This design is only barely keeping up with the current volume, despite relatively low bandwidth utilization.  
  
You are informed that, because of seasonality, the company expects the number of files to double for the next three months. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Introduce data compression for each file to increase the rate file of file transfer.
Contact your internet service provider (ISP) to increase your maximum bandwidth to at least 100 Mbps.
Redesign the data ingestion process to use gsutil tool to send the CSV files to a storage bucket in parallel.
Assemble 1,000 files into a tape archive (TAR) file. Transmit the TAR files instead, and disassemble the CSV files in the cloud upon receiving them.
Create an S3-compatible storage endpoint in your network, and use Google Cloud Storage Transfer Service to transfer on-premises data to the designated storage bucket.

questions.explanation:
For numerous very small files over a high-latency connection, fixed per-transfer and protocol overhead dominates transmission time. Parallel gsutil operations allow multiple uploads to proceed concurrently, while combining 1,000 CSV files into a TAR reduces the number of latency-sensitive transfers by roughly three orders of magnitude. Compression and additional bandwidth do not address the primary latency and per-file-overhead constraint.

**Learn more:** [IAM permissions for gsutil commands](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam-gsutil) · [Transition from gsutil to gcloud storage](https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/gsutil-transition-to-gcloud)

You design a system to analyze seismic data. Your extract, transform, and load (ETL) process runs as a series of MapReduce jobs on an Apache Hadoop cluster. Because some steps are computationally expensive, the ETL process takes days to process a data set. You then discover that a sensor calibration step was omitted. How should you change the ETL process to perform sensor calibration systematically in the future?

options.text: Modify the transformMapReduce jobs to apply sensor calibration before they do anything else.
Introduce a new MapReduce job to apply sensor calibration to raw data, and ensure all other MapReduce jobs are chained after this.
Add sensor calibration data to the output of the ETL process, and document that all users need to apply sensor calibration themselves.
Develop an algorithm through simulation to predict variance of data output from the last MapReduce job based on calibration factors, and apply the correction to all data.

questions.explanation: Sensor calibration should be a dedicated preprocessing MapReduce job that operates on raw data and precedes every downstream job. Chaining all other MapReduce jobs after that stage ensures every subsequent transformation uses consistently calibrated data without duplicating calibration logic across jobs.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You lead BI at a large enterprise with multiple business units, each having distinct priorities and budgets. You use BigQuery on-demand pricing, with a quota of 2K concurrent on-demand slots per project. At times, users in your organization cannot obtain slots to run their queries, and you need to resolve this issue. You want to avoid adding new projects to your account.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Convert your batch BQ queries into interactive BQ queries.
Create an additional project to overcome the 2K on-demand per-project quota.
Switch to flat-rate pricing and establish a hierarchical priority model for your projects.
Increase the amount of concurrent slots per project at the Quotas page at the Cloud Console.

questions.explanation:
BigQuery on-demand workloads are limited to 2,000 slots per project, and that limit cannot be increased through Cloud Customer Care or the quota console. Capacity-based pricing provides configurable reservation capacity, and reservations can be assigned to existing projects to isolate and prioritize workloads across business units.

**Learn more:** [Troubleshoot quota and limit errors | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/troubleshoot-quotas) · [Introduction to workload management | BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reservations-intro)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company’s on-premises Apache Hadoop servers are nearing end-of-life, and IT has chosen to migrate the cluster to Google Cloud Dataproc. A like-for-like cluster migration would need 50 TB of Google Persistent Disk for each node. The CIO is concerned about the expense of using that much block storage. You want to minimize the migration’s storage cost. What should you do?

options.text: Put the data into Google Cloud Storage.
Use preemptible virtual machines (VMs) for the Cloud Dataproc cluster.
Tune the Cloud Dataproc cluster so that there is just enough disk for all data.
Migrate some of the cold data into Google Cloud Storage, and keep only the hot data in Persistent Disk.

questions.explanation:
The Cloud Storage connector lets Apache Hadoop and Spark jobs access data stored directly in Cloud Storage, without first transferring it into HDFS. Storing the dataset in Cloud Storage therefore avoids provisioning 50 TB of Persistent Disk on every Dataproc node, minimizing block-storage cost.

**Learn more:** [Cloud Storage connector | Google Cloud Documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/managed-spark/docs/concepts/connectors/cloud-storage)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a MySQL database workload to Cloud SQL. The database must scale to support several readers across different geographic regions. It must be highly available and satisfy low RTO and RPO requirements, including during a regional outage. You need to minimize reader interruptions during a database failover. What should you do?

options.text: Create a highly available Cloud SQL instance in region Create a highly available read replica in region B. Scale up read workloads by creating cascading read replicas in multiple regions. Backup the Cloud SQL instances to a multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket. Restore the Cloud SQL backup to a new instance in another region when Region A is down.
Create a highly available Cloud SQL instance in region A. Scale up read workloads by creating read replicas in multiple regions. Promote one of the read replicas when region A is down.

Create a highly available Cloud SQL instance in region A. Create a highly available read replica in region B. Scale up read workloads by creating cascading read replicas in multiple regions. Promote the read replica in region B when region A is down.

Create a highly available Cloud SQL instance in region A. Scale up read workloads by creating read replicas in the same region. Failover to the standby Cloud SQL instance when the primary instance fails.

questions.explanation:
A high-availability primary in Region A provides resilience to instance or zonal failures, while a high-availability cross-region replica in Region B provides a promotable disaster-recovery target for a regional outage. Placing cascading read replicas beneath that Region B replica preserves the read tier when it is promoted: its child replicas continue replicating under the new primary, reducing reader disruption and recovery time. Cross-region replication is asynchronous, so RPO is governed by replication lag.

**Learn more:** [About replication in Cloud SQL for MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication) · [Promote replicas for regional migration or disaster recovery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/replication/cross-region-replicas)

The company must upload its historical data to Cloud Storage. Security rules prohibit external IP addresses from accessing its on-premises resources. Following the initial upload, existing on-premises applications will add new data each day. What should they do?

options.text: Execute gsutil rsync from the on-premises servers.
Use Dataflow and write the data to Cloud Storage.
Write a job template in Dataproc to perform the data transfer.
Install an FTP server on a Compute Engine VM to receive the files and move them to Cloud Storage.

questions.explanation:
Running `gsutil rsync` from the on-premises servers lets those servers initiate outbound Cloud Storage API connections, so their resources do not need to accept inbound connections from external IP addresses. Re-running the synchronization on a schedule transfers new or changed files after the initial copy.

questions.question: Your team executes a complex analytical query each day that processes terabytes of data. Recently, the query has failed after running for 20 minutes with a “Resources exceeded” error. You need to fix this issue. What should you do?

options.text: Move from BigQuery on-demand to slot reservations.
Analyze the SQL syntax for errors.
Increase the maximum table size limit.
Increase your project’s BigQuery API request quota.

questions.explanation: A “Resources exceeded” failure during execution indicates that the query lacks sufficient BigQuery compute capacity. Slot reservations provide dedicated query-processing capacity, whereas SQL syntax review, table-size limits, and BigQuery API request quotas do not increase the resources available to execute the query.

questions.question: Your team executes a complex analytical query each day that processes terabytes of data. Recently, the query has failed after running for 20 minutes with a “Resources exceeded” error. You need to fix this issue. What should you do?

options.text: Create a table in BigQuery, and append the new samples for CPU and memory to the table
Create a wide table in BigQuery, create a column for the sample value at each second, and update the row with the interval for each second
Create a narrow table in Bigtable with a row key that combines the Computer Engine computer identifier with the sample time at each second
Create a wide table in Bigtable with a row key that combines the computer identifier with the sample time at each minute, and combine the values for each second as column data.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable is designed for scalable time-series workloads such as CPU and memory usage across many servers. A wide, time-bucketed row groups a computer's per-second measurements for a minute, avoiding a separate narrow row for every sample. Bigtable documents that time-bucket rows improve performance and compression compared with tall, narrow tables, while its sparse column model supports growth as new time-series data is added.

**Learn more:** [Schema design for time series data | Bigtable](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design-time-series) · [Bigtable overview | Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/overview)

questions.question: A company streams real-time sensor data from its factory floor into Bigtable and has observed extremely poor performance. How should it redesign the row key to improve Bigtable performance for queries that populate real-time dashboards?

options.text: Use a row key of the form <timestamp>.
Use a row key of the form <sensorid>.
Use a row key of the form <timestamp>#<sensorid>.
Use a row key of the form >#<sensorid>#<timestamp>.

questions.explanation:
Bigtable row keys should not begin with a timestamp because sequential timestamp values concentrate writes in one key range and create a hotspot. Using the sensor ID first distributes writes across the row-key space, while the trailing timestamp keeps each sensor’s time-series records together for efficient range reads used by real-time dashboards.\
\
**Learn more:** [Schema design best practices | Bigtable | Google Cloud Documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigtable/docs/schema-design)
